energy-changes-in-a-system-and-the-ways-.d: Energy changes in a system, and the ways energy is stored before and after such changes — part 4.1.1.1
terms: A system is an object or group of objects. It is whatever you decide to treat as the thing you are studying — a single ball, or a ball and the Earth, or a kettle together with the water in it. Choosing the system first is what makes it possible to say clearly which stores are emptying and which are filling.

Energy in a system is described as being held in stores. When a system changes, there are changes in the way energy is stored: the amount of energy in some stores goes down and the amount in others goes up.
The energy stores used in this specification

The stores named across the AQA specification are: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, magnetic, electrostatic and nuclear. Heating, work done by forces, work done when a current flows and radiation are not stores — they are the ways energy gets from one store to another.
Describing all the changes in a system

A full description names the store or stores that empty, the store or stores that fill, and the way the energy was transferred between them. 'All the changes' includes the small ones — the thermal stores of the surroundings that fill because of friction or air resistance are part of the answer, not an optional extra.

As the object rises, its kinetic store empties and its gravitational potential store fills; air resistance also fills the thermal store of the object and the surroundings. At the highest point the object is momentarily at rest, so its kinetic store is empty and its gravitational potential store is at its largest. On the way down the changes run the other way.
A moving object hitting an obstacle

The kinetic store of the moving object empties. Energy fills the thermal stores of the object, of the obstacle and of the surroundings, and some is carried away by sound waves. If either object is squashed and springs back, an elastic potential store fills and then empties again.
An object accelerated by a constant force

The force does work on the object as the object moves. Work done by the force fills the kinetic store of the object, so the object speeds up. Because work done = force × distance, acting over a longer distance transfers more energy to the kinetic store, even though the force is unchanged.

The kinetic store of the vehicle empties. Friction forces in the brakes do work, filling the thermal store of the brakes; friction at the tyres and air resistance fill thermal stores too. The hot brakes then transfer energy to the thermal store of the surroundings as they cool.
Bringing water to a boil in an electric kettle

A current flows in the heating element, so work is done and the thermal store of the element fills. The element heats the water, filling the thermal store of the water. The thermal stores of the kettle body and of the surrounding room also fill, and once the water boils, energy is carried away by the escaping steam.
The three ways a system is changed

Throughout the Energy section, the energy change when a system is changed is calculated for three routes: heating, work done by forces, and work done when a current flows. Each is a way of transferring energy into or out of stores, and each is measured in joules.
Calculating an energy change by heating

ΔE = m c Δθ, that is change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change, with ΔE in joules (J), m in kilograms (kg), c in J/kg °C and Δθ in °C. This equation is supplied on the Physics equation sheet, so it does not have to be recalled — but Δθ is the change in temperature, not the final temperature.
Calculating work done by a force

W = F s, that is work done = force × distance (along the line of action of the force), with W in joules (J), F in newtons (N) and s in metres (m). This equation must be recalled. If the object does not move along the line of action of the force, no work is done by that force, however large the force is.
Calculating work done when a current flows

P = E/t, that is power = energy transferred / time, with P in watts (W), E in joules (J) and t in seconds (s). This equation must be recalled, and it rearranges to E = P t. Time must be in seconds: a three-minute boil is 180 s, not 3.

Every energy change — by heating, by work done by forces, or by work done when a current flows — is measured in the same unit, the joule (J). That shared unit is what makes it possible to put all the changes in one system side by side and compare them directly.
Showing redistribution on a common scale

Once each change has been calculated in joules, the amounts can be drawn as bars on one shared scale, showing how the energy in the system was redistributed. The energy is not lost or created: the amounts shown after the change add up to the amount shown before it, spread differently among the stores.

kinetic-energy-elastic-potential-energy-.d: Energy changes in a system, and the ways energy is stored before and after such changes — part 4.1.1.2
terms: The energy stored in an object because it is moving. It is calculated from kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x (speed)^2, that is E_k = 1/2 m v^2, and it is zero when the object is at rest.

In E_k = 1/2 m v^2 the speed alone is squared, not the mass and not the product of the two. Doubling the speed of an object multiplies its kinetic energy by four, while doubling its mass only doubles the kinetic energy.
Units in the kinetic energy equation
Kinetic energy Ek is in joules, J; mass m is in kilograms, kg; speed v is in metres per second, m/s. A mass in grams or a speed in km/h must be converted first, or the answer will not be in joules.

The unit of every energy store in this section: kinetic, elastic potential and gravitational potential energy are all measured in joules. The newton is a unit of force and the watt is a unit of power, so neither can be the unit of an energy calculation.

The energy stored in a spring, or other elastic object, because it has been stretched or compressed. For a spring it is calculated from elastic potential energy = 0.5 x spring constant x (extension)^2, that is E_e = 1/2 k e^2.
A measure of how stiff a spring is: the force needed for each metre of extension. It is measured in newtons per metre, N/m, so a spring of large k needs a large force to stretch it a given amount.

The increase in the length of the spring, measured in metres, m. It is the stretched length minus the original unstretched length, not the stretched length itself, and it must be converted from centimetres or millimetres before it is squared.

The point beyond which extension is no longer proportional to the force applied. The equation E_e = 1/2 k e^2 is used only while the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded; past that point it no longer gives the energy stored.

The energy stored in an object because of its position in a gravitational field. The amount gained when an object is raised is calculated from g.p.e. = mass x gravitational field strength x height, that is E_p = m g h.
The force acting on each kilogram of mass, measured in newtons per kilogram, N/kg. Its value is always supplied in the question in this specification, so it never has to be recalled.

The vertical distance the object is raised above ground level, measured in metres, m. When an object is moved along a slope or a ramp, it is the vertical rise that is used as h, not the longer distance travelled along the surface.
In E_p = m g h the gravitational potential energy Ep is in joules, J; mass m is in kilograms, kg; gravitational field strength g is in newtons per kilogram, N/kg; and height h is in metres, m.
Units in the elastic potential energy equation
In E_e = 1/2 k e^2 the elastic potential energy Ee is in joules, J; the spring constant k is in newtons per metre, N/m; and the extension e is in metres, m.
Mass is the quantity of matter in an object, measured in kilograms, kg, and it is m in all three equations. Weight is a force in newtons and is never substituted for the mass.

Use E_k = 1/2 m v^2 when an object is moving, E_e = 1/2 k e^2 when a spring has been stretched, and E_p = m g h when an object has been raised. Only the kinetic and elastic equations contain a factor of 0.5.

energy-changes-in-a-system-specific-heat.d: Energy changes in a system, and the ways energy is stored before and after such changes — part 4.1.1.3
terms: The object, or group of objects, whose energy is being considered. In this section the system is the material being heated or cooled — for example a metal block, or the water in a beaker.

The amount of energy stored in, or released from, a system as its temperature changes. Change in thermal energy, ∆E, is measured in joules, J. It is a change, not a total: it does not tell you how much energy the system stores altogether.

change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change. This is the equation used to calculate the amount of energy stored in or released from a system as its temperature changes.

∆E = m c ∆θ, where ∆E is the change in thermal energy in joules (J), m is the mass in kilograms (kg), c is the specific heat capacity in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius (J/kg °C) and ∆θ is the temperature change in degrees Celsius (°C). To find the specific heat capacity from measurements the equation is rearranged to c = ∆E ÷ (m ∆θ).

The mass of the material whose temperature changes, symbol m, measured in kilograms, kg. A mass measured in grams must be divided by 1000 before it is substituted into ∆E = m c ∆θ, because the unit of specific heat capacity is per kilogram.
Specific heat capacity (c) and its unit

Specific heat capacity, symbol c, is measured in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C. The unit is read directly from the definition: joules of energy, for each kilogram of substance, for each degree Celsius of temperature rise. It is a property of the substance, so its value does not depend on how much of the substance you have.

The specific heat capacity of a substance is the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius. The word 'specific' means 'per kilogram': the quantity is defined for a fixed one kilogram of the substance, not for the whole sample.

The difference between the final temperature and the starting temperature of the system, symbol ∆θ, measured in degrees Celsius, °C. It is a difference, so the value substituted into the equation is final temperature − starting temperature, never the final temperature on its own.

An investigation to determine the specific heat capacity of one or more materials. In a common version, the mass of a metal block is measured, an immersion heater and a thermometer are placed in the holes in the block, the block is lagged, the starting temperature is recorded, and the energy supplied by the heater and the temperature are recorded as the block warms. The specific heat capacity is then found from c = ∆E ÷ (m ∆θ). A version using a measured mass of water in an insulated container works in the same way.
Linking the energy stores in the practical

The investigation works by linking the decrease of one energy store (or the work done) to the increase in temperature, and so to the increase in the thermal energy stored by the material. With an electric immersion heater, the energy transferred from the supply is taken as the energy transferred to the material; the value of ∆E used in the calculation is that measured energy, read from a joulemeter or found from power × time.
Lagging and energy transferred to the surroundings

Insulating material (lagging) is wrapped round the block or container to reduce the energy transferred from it to the surroundings. Any energy that does escape was measured as supplied but did not raise the material's temperature, so the calculated specific heat capacity comes out higher than the accepted value. Lagging reduces this error; it never removes it completely.

Use of appropriate apparatus to make and record a range of measurements accurately, including mass, time and temperature. Here it means using a balance to measure the mass of the block or the water, and a thermometer or temperature sensor to record temperatures, with sensible precision and at recorded time intervals.

Safe use of appropriate apparatus to measure energy changes and transfers. Here it means setting up and using the immersion heater, the low voltage supply and the joulemeter (or ammeter, voltmeter and timer) safely — the heater must be in the block or water before it is switched on, and the hot block must not be handled — and using them to measure the energy transferred.

Opportunities include identifying the variables (energy supplied and temperature measured; mass and material controlled), evaluating the method by identifying energy transferred to the surroundings as a source of error, suggesting improvements such as better lagging or a smaller temperature range, and judging the result by comparing it with an accepted value for the material.

Opportunities include converting a mass in grams to kilograms, calculating ∆θ as a difference of two readings, rearranging ∆E = m c ∆θ to make c the subject, quoting the answer to a sensible number of significant figures with the unit J/kg °C, and plotting temperature against energy supplied and using the gradient of the straight line, which equals 1 ÷ (m c).

energy-changes-in-a-system-power.d: Energy changes in a system, and the ways energy is stored before and after such changes — part 4.1.1.4
terms: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred, or the rate at which work is done. It is not a quantity of energy: it says how many joules are transferred each second, so a power value always needs both an energy and a time.
The watt is the unit of power, symbol W. An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is equal to a power of 1 watt, so 1 W is 1 J/s.
The energy transferred, symbol E, is measured in joules, J. Divided by the time in seconds it gives the power: power = (energy transferred)/(time), [P = E/t].

Work done, symbol W, is measured in joules, J, because doing work is one way of transferring energy. Divided by the time it gives the power: power = (work done)/(time), [P = W/t]. The letter W is also the symbol for the watt; in P = W/t it stands for the work done.
The time, symbol t, is measured in seconds, s. A time given in minutes or hours must be converted to seconds before it is used in P = E/t or P = W/t.

Two machines that transfer the same energy, for example two electric motors lifting the same weight through the same height, differ in power only through the time taken. The one that finishes sooner has the greater power.
Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but it cannot be created or destroyed. The total energy before a change is always equal to the total energy after it.
A system in which no energy enters or leaves. Energy can still be transferred between the stores inside a closed system, but there is no net change to the total energy of the system.
The spreading out of energy into stores that are less useful, most often the thermal store of the surroundings. Energy is dissipated in all system changes.

The everyday name for energy that has been dissipated. It has not been destroyed; it has been stored in a way that cannot be used for the intended purpose, for example in the thermal store of a warm motor.
Putting a substance such as oil between surfaces that move over each other. The friction between the surfaces is reduced, so less energy is dissipated to thermal stores as the machine runs.
A layer of material of low thermal conductivity placed around an object or a building to reduce the rate of energy transfer by conduction to the surroundings.
A property of a material, used here only as a comparison: the higher the thermal conductivity of a material, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across the material.
Rate of cooling of a building
How quickly a building transfers energy to colder surroundings. The rate of cooling is lower when the walls are thicker and when the walls are made of a material with a lower thermal conductivity.

An investigation of the effectiveness of different materials as thermal insulators, and of the factors that affect the thermal insulation properties of a material, such as the thickness of the layer and the number of layers used.
Control variables in the insulation practical

The quantities kept the same so that only the material or the thickness affects the result: the volume and starting temperature of the water, the size of the container, the room temperature and the time over which the temperature is measured.
AT 1 and AT 5 in this practical

AT 1 is the use of appropriate apparatus to make and record measurements of length, temperature and time; AT 5 is making measurements of energy and temperature changes. Both are exercised by measuring the thickness of the insulating layer with a ruler and by recording the fall in water temperature at set times.

Working scientifically and mathematical skills developed in this practical: taking repeat readings for each material, identifying anomalous results, calculating a mean temperature drop and plotting the results so that materials can be compared.

The share of the energy supplied to a device that is transferred usefully. The energy efficiency for any energy transfer can be calculated using the equation: efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer). Efficiency is a ratio, so it has no unit and can never be greater than 1.
Efficiency may also be calculated using the equation: efficiency = (useful power output)/(total power input). Both powers must be in the same unit, and the answer is again a ratio with no unit.

Making a larger share of the input energy transfer useful by reducing the unwanted transfers: lubricating moving parts, insulating hot components, streamlining a moving object to reduce air resistance and using thicker wires of lower resistance.

A supply of energy that people can draw on. The main energy resources available for use on Earth include fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), nuclear fuel, bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves. Electricity is not an energy resource: it has to be generated using one of these resources.

The three fossil fuels named by the specification. They formed from the remains of living things over many millions of years and are burned to release energy. They are non-renewable: they are not replenished on any timescale that matters against the rate at which they are used.
Uranium (or plutonium) used as a fuel in nuclear power stations. It is mined from rock but it is not a fossil fuel, and it is non-renewable because the fuel is not replenished as it is used.
Fuel made from plant or animal material, for example wood, crops grown for fuel, or waste. It is renewable because the crops used can be grown again as the fuel is used.

Moving air, used as an energy resource mainly for electricity generation. It is renewable, and it is unreliable in the sense that its output rises and falls with the weather and cannot be turned up on demand.

An energy resource that uses water stored behind a dam, usually in a river valley. It is renewable, because rain refills the reservoir, and it is comparatively reliable because the stored water can be released when it is wanted.
An energy resource that uses the energy of hot rock beneath the Earth's surface. It is renewable and available at all hours, but it is only practical where hot rock lies close enough to the surface.

The twice-daily rise and fall of the sea, caused by the Moon and the Sun rather than by the weather. Tidal energy is renewable and reliable, because the times of high and low water are known in advance.

The Sun is an energy resource in its own right. Its energy can be used for heating (for example warming water directly) as well as for electricity generation. It is renewable, and its output varies with the time of day, the season and the cloud.
Waves on the surface of the sea, raised by the wind. Wave energy is renewable and is a separate resource from both hydro-electricity and the tides.

A renewable energy resource is one that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used. The test is replacement keeping pace with use - not the size of the supply, not the price, and not whether the resource is clean.
A resource that is not replenished as it is used, so the supply falls as it is drawn on. Coal, oil, gas and nuclear fuel are non-renewable.
Moving people and goods. Worldwide, transport runs overwhelmingly on oil, as petrol and diesel; bio-fuel and electricity supply smaller shares.
Producing electricity for the mains supply. Almost every resource on the specification's list can be used this way, which is why electricity itself is not a resource.
Warming homes, water and industrial processes. Gas, oil, bio-fuel, geothermal and the Sun are all used for heating directly, without any electricity being generated first.

How dependably a resource can supply energy when it is wanted. Fossil fuels, nuclear fuel and geothermal can be run whenever they are needed; the tides are predictable in advance; wind, the Sun and water waves depend on the weather. Reliability is about availability on demand, not about how much energy the resource gives out.

The damage done by obtaining and using a resource: carbon dioxide from burning fuels, sulfur dioxide leading to acid rain, radioactive waste from nuclear fuel, and land, habitat and landscape effects from dams, wind farms and fuel crops. Every resource has some impact.
Trends in the use of energy resources

Patterns over time, such as the rising share of wind and solar, the decline of coal, and the continued dominance of oil in transport. Trends are driven by cost, by concern about environmental impact and by government decisions.
Political, social, ethical and economic considerations

The non-scientific factors that decide whether an environmental issue is acted on. Science can identify an issue but does not always have the power to deal with it, because cost, jobs, public opinion, fairness between countries and government policy all bear on what is actually done.

Circuit diagrams use standard symbols, so that any circuit can be read by anyone. The symbols needed are: open switch, closed switch, cell, battery, diode, resistor, variable resistor, LED, lamp, fuse, voltmeter, ammeter, thermistor and LDR. A cell is one long thin line beside one short thick line; a battery is two or more cells drawn in line. A resistor is a plain rectangle; a variable resistor is that rectangle with an arrow drawn diagonally across it. An ammeter is a circle containing A; a voltmeter is a circle containing V.

To draw a circuit diagram, components are joined by straight lines standing for connecting wires, with each component shown by its correct standard symbol. To interpret one, trace the loops: components on the same single loop are in series and carry the same current, while components on separate branches are in parallel. An ammeter is always drawn in the loop with the component whose current is being measured; a voltmeter is always drawn as a separate branch across the component.

For electrical charge to flow through a closed circuit the circuit must include a source of potential difference, such as a cell, a battery or a power supply. A complete loop on its own is not enough: with nothing to push the charges round, the current is zero. The source does not create the charges — they are already in the metal — it provides the potential difference that makes them drift one way.

Electric current is a flow of electrical charge. The size of the electric current is the rate of flow of electrical charge, that is, how much charge passes a point each second. It is not a flow of energy, and it is not the speed of the individual electrons, which drift very slowly even when the current is large.
Charge flow equation Q = I t

Charge flow, current and time are linked by the equation charge flow = current × time, written [Q = I t]. Rearranged, I = Q ÷ t and t = Q ÷ I. The time must be in seconds before it is substituted, so minutes and hours have to be converted first: 5.0 minutes is 300 s.
Charge flow, Q, is measured in coulombs, C. The coulomb is a quantity of charge, not a rate: one coulomb passes a point when a current of one ampere flows for one second.

Current, I, is measured in amperes, A; amp is acceptable for ampere. One ampere is a flow of one coulomb of charge each second, so the ampere measures a rate of flow of charge while the coulomb measures an amount of charge.

Time, t, is measured in seconds, s. Because the equations of this section are defined with time in seconds, any time given in minutes or hours must be converted before substitution: multiply minutes by 60 and hours by 3600.
Current in a single closed loop

A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop. Charge is not used up as it goes round, so an ammeter placed anywhere in that loop gives the same reading, whether it is before, between or after the components. What the components use is energy, not charge.

The current through a component depends on both the resistance of the component and the potential difference across it. Resistance opposes the flow of charge: the greater the resistance of the component, the smaller the current for a given pd across it. The current can therefore be changed either by changing the pd or by changing the resistance.

Potential difference, V, is measured in volts, V. It is the quantity that drives charge round a circuit, and it is measured across a component rather than through it. Questions are set using the term potential difference; a student who writes voltage instead gains credit, because voltage is an accepted alternative name for the same quantity.

Current, potential difference or resistance can be calculated using the equation potential difference = current × resistance, written [V = I R]. Rearranged, I = V ÷ R and R = V ÷ I. To find a resistance you divide the pd by the current; multiplying them instead is the commonest error in this topic.

Resistance, R, is measured in ohms, Ω. One ohm is the resistance of a component that has a pd of one volt across it when a current of one ampere passes through it, which follows directly from R = V ÷ I.

Circuit diagrams are used to set up and check appropriate circuits to investigate the factors affecting the resistance of electrical circuits. The standard arrangement puts an ammeter in the loop with the test component and a voltmeter across it; the resistance is then calculated from R = V ÷ I. The two factors investigated are the length of a wire at constant temperature, and combinations of resistors in series and parallel.
Resistance and the length of a wire

For a wire at constant temperature, resistance is directly proportional to length: doubling the length doubles the resistance, and a graph of resistance against length is a straight line through the origin. The temperature must be held constant, which is why the current is kept small and the circuit is switched off between readings — a wire that warms up has a higher resistance, which would spoil the pattern.
Resistors in series and in parallel

Resistors joined in series have a combined resistance larger than either one alone, because the charge must pass through both. Resistors joined in parallel have a combined resistance smaller than either one alone, because the charge now has more than one path to take; two identical resistors in parallel give half the resistance of one.

The current through an ohmic conductor at a constant temperature is directly proportional to the potential difference across the resistor, which means that the resistance remains constant as the current changes. Its I–V graph is a straight line through the origin. A fixed resistor kept at constant temperature is the standard example.

For some resistors the value of R remains constant, but in others it can change as the current changes. The resistance of components such as lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs is not constant; it changes with the current through the component. Their I–V graphs are therefore not straight lines through the origin.

The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases. A larger current heats the filament more, so its resistance rises and its I–V graph bends over into an S-shape, becoming less steep as the pd increases. A filament lamp is therefore not an ohmic conductor.

The current through a diode flows in one direction only. The diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction, so the reverse current is very nearly zero. In the forward direction it conducts, but only once the pd is large enough, so its I–V graph lies flat along the reverse side and then rises steeply forward.

The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases. This is the opposite of the behaviour of a metal wire, whose resistance rises when it is heated, and it is what makes the thermistor useful as a temperature sensor.

In a thermostat the thermistor senses the room temperature. When the room cools, the thermistor's resistance rises; the circuit detects that change and switches the heater on. When the room warms again the resistance falls and the heater is switched off, so the temperature is held near a set value. The same idea is used in fire alarms and in engine temperature sensors.

The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases. In bright light its resistance may be only a few hundred ohms; in darkness it can be millions of ohms. It is therefore used as a light sensor.

An LDR is used to switch lights on when it gets dark. As darkness falls, the light intensity on the LDR drops, so its resistance rises; the circuit senses that change and switches the street lamp on. At dawn the resistance falls again and the lamp is switched off. The same arrangement is used in automatic camera exposure and in burglar alarms.

To measure the resistance of a component, an ammeter is placed in the loop with the component so that it measures the current through it, and a voltmeter is placed across the component so that it measures the potential difference across it. The resistance is then calculated from R = V ÷ I. The circuit diagram is drawn using correct circuit symbols; a variable resistor or a variable power supply lets several pairs of readings be taken.

Graphs are used to explore whether circuit elements are linear or non-linear. A linear element gives a straight-line I–V graph through the origin and has constant resistance; a non-linear element gives a curve, and its resistance changes. The shape relates to the function of the component: the lamp's curve flattens because the filament heats up, and the diode's graph is flat on one side because it conducts one way only.

Circuit diagrams are used to construct appropriate circuits to investigate the I–V characteristics of a variety of circuit elements, including a filament lamp, a diode and a resistor at constant temperature. Readings of current and pd are taken over a range of values, including reversed ones, and plotted as I against V. The resistor must be kept at constant temperature so that heating does not change the resistance being measured.

Components are in series when they are joined one after another in a single loop, so there is only one path for charge. Every charge that passes through one component must pass through all the others.
Components are in parallel when they are joined side by side between the same two points, so the charge has a choice of paths. Each component sits on its own branch of the circuit.
A point in a circuit where the conducting path divides or rejoins. Charge that arrives at a junction each second equals the charge that leaves it each second, so no charge is created or lost there.
In series there is the same current through each component, because there is only one path and charge is not used up. Moving an ammeter to a different place in the loop does not change its reading.
Sharing of potential difference in series
The total potential difference of the power supply is shared between components connected in series, so the separate potential differences add up to the supply potential difference.
The total resistance of two components in series is the sum of the resistance of each component, R_total = R_1 + R_2, because the charge has to pass through both in turn.
The potential difference across each component connected in parallel is the same, because the ends of every branch are joined to the same two points in the circuit.
Total current in a parallel circuit
The total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components, because the current from the supply divides between the branches and rejoins afterwards.
The total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor, because the second resistor gives the charge an extra path to flow along.
The unit of resistance, R, is the ohm, symbol Ω. A component has a resistance of one ohm when a potential difference of one volt across it drives a current of one ampere through it.
A single resistance that could replace a group of resistors without changing the current drawn from the supply. For resistors in series it is found by adding the individual resistances.
An ammeter measures current and is connected in series with the component whose current is wanted, so that the same current passes through both the meter and that component.
A voltmeter measures potential difference and is connected in parallel with the component, that is across its two ends, so it experiences the same potential difference as that component.
A direct current supply, such as a cell or battery, drives charge around the circuit in one direction only. The dc series circuits used for measurement and testing are built from such a supply.
A circuit that contains both series and parallel parts, for example a resistor in series with a pair of lamps that are in parallel with each other.
Variable resistor in a test circuit
A resistor whose resistance can be changed. Placed in series in a test circuit it alters the current, so several pairs of current and potential difference readings can be taken for one component.
A supply in which the potential difference repeatedly changes direction, so the current it drives repeatedly reverses direction. Mains electricity is an ac supply.
A potential difference that is always in the same direction, so the current it drives passes round the circuit in one direction only. Cells and batteries supply a direct potential difference.

The frequency of an ac supply is the number of complete cycles of the alternating potential difference each second, measured in hertz (Hz). In the United Kingdom the domestic supply has a frequency of 50 Hz.
Mains potential difference in the UK
The United Kingdom domestic electricity supply is about 230 V. This is the potential difference the live wire carries relative to earth.
The cable used to connect most electrical appliances to the mains. It contains three separately insulated wires: the live wire, the neutral wire and the earth wire.
The wire with brown insulation. It carries the alternating potential difference from the supply, and is at about 230 V relative to earth.
The wire with blue insulation. It completes the circuit, and is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V).
The wire with green and yellow striped insulation. It is a safety wire to stop the appliance becoming live. It is at 0 V and only carries a current if there is a fault.
The insulation covering each wire in a mains cable is colour coded for easy identification: live wire brown, neutral wire blue, earth wire green and yellow stripes.
The potential of the ground, taken as 0 V. Potential differences in a mains circuit are measured relative to this zero.
Potential difference between live and earth
The potential difference between the live wire and earth (0 V) is about 230 V. This is what drives a current through anything that connects the live wire to earth.

The neutral wire is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V). This is why the potential difference across an appliance is about 230 V even though only one of its two supply wires is at a high potential.

A fault in which the live wire comes into contact with a conducting part of an appliance, such as a metal case, so that part is raised to about 230 V. The earth wire is the safety wire that stops this happening.
Danger from a live wire with the switch open

Opening a switch in the mains circuit breaks the circuit, but the live wire on the supply side of the switch is still connected to the supply and is still at about 230 V relative to earth. Touching it is therefore still dangerous.

Any connection between the live wire and earth places about 230 V across that path. If the path is a person, or a low-resistance conductor, a large current passes through it, which is why such connections are dangerous.
Power transfer in a circuit device
The power of a circuit device is the rate at which it transfers energy, that is the energy it transfers each second. A device with a larger power transfers more energy in the same time.
The power transferred by a circuit device is found by multiplying the potential difference across the device by the current through it: power = potential difference x current.
The symbol form of power = potential difference x current, where P is power in watts, V is potential difference in volts and I is current in amperes.

The power transferred by a circuit device can also be found from the current through it and its resistance: power = (current)^2 x resistance. The current is squared, so the power is very sensitive to the current.
The symbol form of power = (current)^2 x resistance, where P is power in watts, I is current in amperes and R is resistance in ohms.
Power, P, is measured in watts, W. One watt is an energy transfer of one joule each second, so a 60 W lamp transfers 60 J of energy every second it is switched on.
Potential difference, V, is measured in volts, V. One volt is one joule of energy transferred per coulomb of charge that flows.
Current, I, is measured in amperes, A, and amp is acceptable for ampere. A current of one ampere is a charge flow of one coulomb each second.
Resistance, R, is measured in ohms. Resistance opposes the flow of charge in a circuit, and for a given current a larger resistance means a larger power transfer.
An everyday electrical appliance such as a kettle, a lamp or a food mixer is designed to bring about a particular energy transfer when a current flows through it.
The amount of energy an appliance transfers depends on two things: how long the appliance is switched on for, and the power of the appliance.
In appliances such as a food mixer, a drill or a washing machine, energy is transferred electrically from batteries or the ac mains to the kinetic energy of an electric motor.
In appliances such as a kettle, a toaster or an iron, energy is transferred electrically from the ac mains to a heating device, raising the temperature of water, food or metal.
Portable appliances are usually supplied by batteries, which provide a direct current. Appliances plugged into sockets are supplied by the ac mains.
Work is done when charge flows in a circuit. The energy transferred by that work comes from the store associated with the source, such as the chemical store of a battery.
The energy transferred by electrical work can be calculated from the power of the device and the time for which it operates: energy transferred = power x time.
The symbol form of energy transferred = power x time, where E is energy transferred in joules, P is power in watts and t is time in seconds.
energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference
The energy transferred by electrical work can also be calculated from the charge that flows and the potential difference it moves through: energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference.
The symbol form of energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference, where E is energy transferred in joules, Q is charge flow in coulombs and V is potential difference in volts.
Energy transferred, E, is measured in joules, J. One joule is transferred when a power of one watt operates for one second.
Time, t, is measured in seconds, s, in E = P t. Times given in minutes or hours must be converted to seconds before the equation is used.
Charge flow, Q, is measured in coulombs, C. A charge flow of one coulomb passes when a current of one ampere flows for one second.
Energy transferred over a given time

Because energy transferred = power x time, the power of a device is the energy it transfers divided by the time in seconds. Two devices can transfer the same energy at different powers if they run for different times.

The power rating printed on an appliance is the power it transfers when working normally. A higher power rating means a faster change in the stored energy of the appliance and its surroundings while it is in use.
The National Grid is a system of cables and transformers that links power stations to consumers such as homes, schools and factories.
A step-up transformer increases the potential difference from the power station to the transmission cables, which reduces the current in those cables for the same power.
A step-down transformer decreases the potential difference, to a much lower value, for domestic use, so that mains electricity reaches consumers at a safe potential difference.
Transmitting at a high potential difference means a low current in the cables. Because the power wasted by heating the cables is given by P = I^2 R, a lower current wastes much less energy.
Electric charge that has built up on an object and stays where it is instead of flowing as a current. It is produced when certain insulating materials are rubbed against each other.
When two insulating materials are rubbed together, electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other, leaving both materials charged.
The movement of negatively charged electrons from one material to another. No charge is created or destroyed; it is only moved.
An object that has gained electrons, so it has more electrons than the positive charge in it can balance.
An object that has lost electrons, so the positive charge left in it is no longer balanced.
The charges produced by rubbing are always equal in size and opposite in sign, because every electron lost by one material is gained by the other.
A material through which charge cannot flow easily, so charge placed on it stays where it is put. Charging by rubbing works with certain insulating materials.
Two objects that carry the same type of charge push each other apart.
Two objects that carry different types of charge pull each other together.
A force that acts between two objects that are not touching. Attraction and repulsion between charged objects are examples of a non-contact force.
A sudden flow of charge across a gap, seen and heard as a spark, which happens when enough charge has built up on a surface.
When the electric field in a gap becomes strong enough, the air in the gap stops behaving as an insulator and allows charge to flow across, producing a spark.
The region around a charged object in which a second charged object experiences a force.
The electric field is strongest close to the charged object and gets weaker the further away from it you go.
Field pattern for an isolated charged sphere

Straight field lines spreading out radially in all directions from the sphere, evenly spaced around it and closer together near the surface, with arrows pointing away from a positive sphere and towards a negative one.
Force on a second charged object
A charged object placed in an electric field experiences a force, and that force gets stronger as the distance between the two objects decreases.
Field explanation of a non-contact force
Each charged object sits inside the electric field of the other, so each one experiences a force without the two ever touching.
A charged rod hung on a thread so that it can turn freely, used as evidence that a second charged rod brought near it, but not touching, can push it away or pull it round.

changes-of-state-and-the-particle-model.d: Changes of state and the particle model
terms: Density is how much mass a material packs into each unit of volume. Because it is a ratio, it belongs to the material rather than to the lump of material: a small piece and a large piece of the same metal at the same temperature have the same density.
The specification defines density by density = mass / volume. Mass goes on the top and volume on the bottom, so for a fixed mass a larger volume always means a smaller density.

In the symbol form of the equation, written as rho = m/V, rho stands for density, m stands for mass and V stands for volume. The symbols are not initials of the words, which is why they have to be learned.
The specification gives density, rho, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m^3. The unit follows straight from the equation: a mass in kilograms divided by a volume in metres cubed.
Mass, m, is measured in kilograms, kg. A balance usually reads in grams, so a reading in grams must be divided by 1000 before it is used to obtain a density in kg/m^3.
Volume, V, is measured in metres cubed, m^3. For a regular solid the volume is found by multiplying length by width by height. A volume in cm^3 must be divided by 1 000 000 to convert it to m^3.
One gram per centimetre cubed is one thousand kilograms per metre cubed, so a density in g/cm^3 is multiplied by 1000 to give kg/m^3. Water is 1.0 g/cm^3, which is 1000 kg/m^3.

The particle model pictures a substance as a very large number of tiny particles in constant motion. Their spacing and arrangement explain both the three states of matter and the differences in density between those states.
In a solid the particles are packed closely together in a fixed, regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions. A solid therefore keeps its own shape and has a fixed volume.

In a liquid the particles are still close together and touching, but the arrangement is random and the particles can move past one another. A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container.
In a gas the particles are far apart, arranged randomly and moving quickly in all directions. A gas has no fixed shape or volume and fills whatever container it is put in.

A simple diagram uses identical circles for the particles. A solid is drawn as circles touching in a regular pattern, a liquid as circles touching in a random pattern, and a gas as widely separated circles. The circles are the same size in all three diagrams.

For the same substance the particles have the same mass in every state, so density depends only on how closely they are packed. Solids and liquids have similar, high densities; a gas has a much lower density because the same particles are spread through a far larger volume.

For a regularly shaped object the mass is found on a balance and the volume is calculated from measured dimensions, for example length x width x height for a cuboid. Density is then the mass divided by that volume.

For an irregularly shaped object the volume is found by lowering it into a measuring cylinder of water, or into a displacement can, and recording the volume of water pushed out of the way. The volume of the object is the rise in level, that is the final reading minus the starting reading.

The mass of the empty measuring cylinder is recorded, a measured volume of liquid is poured in, and the cylinder is weighed again. The mass of the liquid is the difference between the two readings, and that mass is divided by the measured volume.

A ruler is suitable for lengths of a few centimetres, Vernier callipers resolve to about 0.1 mm and suit small objects, and a micrometer resolves to about 0.01 mm and suits thin wires and sheets. The instrument is chosen so that its resolution is small compared with the length being measured.
Melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing and subliming are changes of state. The particles gain or lose energy and rearrange, but no particles are created or destroyed.
Conservation of mass in a change of state

When a substance changes state the number of particles and the mass of each particle are unchanged, so the total mass is unchanged. A balance reading only falls because gas has escaped from the container, not because mass has vanished.

A change of state is a physical change: no new substance is made, and reversing the change returns the material to its original properties. In a chemical change new substances are formed and the original properties are not recovered by simply reversing the conditions.
The energy stored inside a system by the particles (atoms and molecules) that make up that system. It is a store held by the particles, not a fluid that enters or leaves the system.
The energy the particles have because they are moving, vibrating or rotating. It is one of the two contributions to internal energy, and it is the contribution linked to temperature.

The energy stored because of the positions of the particles relative to one another and the forces between them. It is the second contribution to internal energy, and it is the store that changes during a change of state.
An energy transfer that increases the energy of the particles that make up a system. The result is either a rise in the temperature of the system or a change of state.
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change, written in symbols as ∆E = m c ∆θ. It applies when heating or cooling changes the temperature of a substance.
Change in thermal energy, ∆E, is in joules, J; mass, m, is in kilograms, kg; temperature change, ∆θ, is in degrees Celsius, °C.
Specific heat capacity, c, is measured in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C, because it is an energy quoted for each kilogram and for each degree Celsius of temperature change.
The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius.
A change between solid, liquid and vapour in which the substance stays the same substance. While it happens the temperature does not change, even though energy is still being transferred.
The energy needed for a substance to change state. It changes the energy stored (internal energy) of the substance but not its temperature.
The amount of energy required to change the state of one kilogram of a substance with no change in temperature. Energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat, or E = m L.
Energy, E, is in joules, J; mass, m, is in kilograms, kg; specific latent heat, L, is in joules per kilogram, J/kg. No temperature unit appears because the temperature does not change.
The specific latent heat for the change of state from solid to liquid, that is for melting, and in reverse for freezing.
The specific latent heat for the change of state from liquid to vapour, that is for boiling, and in reverse for condensing.

A graph of temperature against time for a substance heated or cooled at a steady rate. Sloping sections show the temperature changing within one state; flat sections show a change of state, where energy is still transferred but the temperature is constant.

The molecules of a gas are in constant random motion. They travel in all directions and at a wide range of speeds, changing direction whenever they collide with each other or with the walls of the container. No molecule keeps one path or one speed for long.

The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules. Raising the temperature raises that average, so the molecules move faster on average. Individual molecules still have a range of speeds; temperature describes the average, not any one molecule.

Gas pressure arises from the collisions of the moving gas molecules with the walls of the container. Each collision exerts a small force on the wall; the huge number of collisions every second adds up to a steady net force spread over the wall area.

A gas is at constant volume when it is sealed in a rigid container that cannot expand or contract, so the space the gas occupies cannot change. Only the temperature and the pressure are free to change.
Pressure and temperature at constant volume

Changing the temperature of a gas held at constant volume changes the pressure it exerts. Heating raises the average kinetic energy, so the molecules hit the walls more frequently and with more force, and the pressure rises. Cooling has the opposite effect.
Net force at right angles to a surface

The pressure of a gas produces a net force at right angles to the wall of the gas container, or to any surface in contact with the gas. Molecules arrive from every direction, so the sideways parts of their impacts cancel out and only the component perpendicular to the surface remains.
Compression and expansion of a gas

A gas can be compressed or expanded by pressure changes. Unlike a solid or a liquid, the molecules of a gas are far apart, so the volume the gas occupies can be squeezed down or allowed to grow when the pressure acting on it changes.

If a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature is given a larger volume, the molecules keep the same average kinetic energy but are spread through a bigger space. Each molecule travels further between wall collisions, so fewer collisions happen each second on each square metre of wall, and the pressure falls.
Fixed mass of gas at constant temperature

The condition under which pressure × volume = constant holds. The same molecules must stay sealed in the container, with none added or lost, and the temperature must not change. If gas escapes or the temperature changes, the relationship no longer applies.

For a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature, pressure × volume = constant, written as [p V = constant]. Pressure and volume change in opposite directions: doubling the pressure halves the volume, and tripling the volume divides the pressure by three.

The unit of pressure. In the relationship p V = constant the pressure, p, is in pascals, Pa. One pascal is one newton per square metre, so a pressure is a force spread over an area, not a force on its own.

The unit of volume used in this relationship: volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3. Volumes quoted in cubic centimetres or in litres must be converted to m^3 before they are used alongside pressures in pascals.
Using p V = constant in a calculation

Because p V has the same value before and after the change, the initial pressure × the initial volume equals the final pressure × the final volume. Multiply the two quantities you know together, then divide by the third to find the missing pressure or the missing volume.
Work is the transfer of energy by a force. When a force moves something, energy is transferred from one store to another, and the amount of energy transferred is the work done.

The energy stored by the molecules of a gas, made up of the kinetic energy of their motion and the potential energy of their positions. Doing work on a gas increases the internal energy of the gas and can cause an increase in the temperature of the gas.
Doing work on an enclosed gas

When a force pushes a piston into a sealed gas, the piston moves while pushing on the gas, so work is done on the gas. That transfer increases the internal energy of the gas, which can raise its temperature — this is why the barrel of a bicycle pump becomes warm in use.
The process in which an unstable nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable. It is a random process.
A nucleus that will give out radiation at some point because its present combination of protons and neutrons is not stable.
A process in which it is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next, or when a particular nucleus will decay. Only the average behaviour of a large number of nuclei is predictable.
The rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays.
The unit in which activity is measured. One becquerel is one decay each second.
The number of decays recorded each second by a detector. It is smaller than the activity of the source, because a detector only intercepts some of the radiation emitted.
A detector of nuclear radiation. Each particle or ray it absorbs produces a pulse, and the pulses are counted to give a count-rate.
The radiation emitted by an unstable nucleus. It may be an alpha particle, a beta particle, a gamma ray or a neutron.
A particle emitted from a nucleus consisting of two neutrons and two protons; it is the same as a helium nucleus.
A high speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton.
Electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus.
The emission of a neutron from an unstable nucleus. It is one of the types of nuclear radiation listed by the specification.
How far radiation travels into a material before it is absorbed. Alpha is stopped by paper or skin, beta by a few millimetres of aluminium, and gamma is only reduced by thick lead or concrete.
How far radiation travels through air before it is absorbed. Alpha travels a few centimetres, beta about a metre, and gamma travels a very long way.
How strongly radiation removes electrons from the atoms it passes. Alpha is the most ionising, beta is weaker, and gamma is the least ionising.
An equation used to represent radioactive decay, showing the parent nucleus on the left and the products of the decay on the right.
The top number in a nuclear symbol, giving the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. It must balance across a nuclear equation.
The bottom number in a nuclear symbol, giving the number of protons and therefore the charge of the nucleus. It must balance across a nuclear equation.
Alpha decay causes both the mass and the charge of the nucleus to decrease: the mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number falls by 2.
Beta decay does not cause the mass of the nucleus to change but does cause the charge of the nucleus to increase: the atomic number rises by 1.
The emission of a gamma ray does not cause the mass or the charge of the nucleus to change.
Choosing the mass numbers and atomic numbers so that the total mass number and the total atomic number are the same on both sides of the equation.
The time it takes for the number of nuclei of an isotope in a sample to halve, or the time it takes for the count rate or activity from the sample to fall to half its initial level.
After n half-lives the emission has fallen by a factor of 2 to the power n, so the net decline is written as the ratio 1 : 2 to the power n.
The unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials. The hazard is due to the decay of the contaminating atoms.
The process of exposing an object to nuclear radiation. The irradiated object does not become radioactive.

Steps such as handling a source with tongs, keeping it at a distance, limiting exposure time and storing it in a lead-lined container, taken to protect against any hazard the source used for irradiation may present.
The checking of published findings by other scientists. It is why studies of the effects of radiation on humans must be published and shared.
Choosing a source for a use

Selecting the radiation whose penetration, range in air and ionising power suit the job: alpha where the radiation must be absorbed over a short distance, beta where it must pass through thin material, gamma where it must pass through thick material or out of a body.
In a nuclear equation an alpha particle may be represented by the symbol ⁴₂He, with mass number 4 written above and atomic number 2 below.
In a nuclear equation a beta particle is represented by the symbol ⁰₋₁e, with mass number 0 written above and charge −1 below.

hazards-and-uses-of-radioactive-emission.d: Hazards and uses of radioactive emissions and of background radiation (physics only)
terms: The low-level ionising radiation that is around us all of the time. It comes from natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space, and from man-made sources such as the fallout from nuclear weapons testing and nuclear accidents.

Sources that are not the result of human activity, such as rocks and cosmic rays from space. Rocks in the ground and in building materials contain radioactive isotopes, so some radiation is always present.

Ionising radiation that arrives at the Earth from space. The atmosphere absorbs much of it, so the dose from cosmic rays is greater at high altitude than at sea level. Cosmic rays are a natural source of background radiation.
Sources that are present because of human activity, such as the fallout from nuclear weapons testing and from nuclear accidents. They add to the natural background rather than replacing it.

Radioactive material thrown into the atmosphere by nuclear weapons testing or by a nuclear accident, which then settles onto the ground and onto vegetation over a wide area. Fallout is a man-made source of background radiation.
Effect of occupation on radiation dose

Some jobs bring extra exposure to radiation, so the dose a person receives depends partly on their occupation. Radiographers, nuclear industry workers and aircrew, for example, receive higher annual doses than most other workers.
Effect of location on radiation dose

The level of background radiation varies from place to place, so dose depends partly on where a person lives or travels. Ground and buildings of granite release more radon gas, and exposure to cosmic rays rises with altitude.
A measure of the risk of harm to body tissue as a result of exposure to ionising radiation. It depends on both the amount of radiation absorbed and the type of radiation the body has been exposed to.
The unit in which radiation dose is measured. A dose stated in sieverts describes the risk to the body, not how radioactive a source is; the activity of a source is measured separately in becquerels.
A smaller unit of radiation dose, used because everyday doses are far below one sievert. 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), so a dose given in mSv is divided by 1000 to convert it into Sv.
Radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-life values, from small fractions of a second for some isotopes to many thousands of millions of years for others.

The hazard from a radioactive material depends on its half-life. A short half-life means a high activity that falls away quickly, so the material is intensely radioactive at first but soon becomes much safer. A long half-life means a lower activity that persists, so the material stays hazardous for a very long time.
Nuclear radiations are used in medicine for the exploration of internal organs and for the control or destruction of unwanted tissue.

A substance containing a radioactive isotope that is taken into the body so that an internal organ can be explored. A gamma emitter with a short half-life is used, because gamma radiation passes out of the body to a detector and the activity soon falls away.

The use of nuclear radiation to control or destroy unwanted tissue such as a tumour. A high dose of gamma radiation is directed at the tumour from outside the body, or an implanted source is placed so that the dose is concentrated where it is needed.

The risk people believe a nuclear radiation carries is often different from the risk shown by data. Evaluating a medical use means comparing the dose received, and its consequences, with the benefit of the diagnosis or treatment and with the risk of doing nothing.
The splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, for example a uranium or a plutonium nucleus. It is a change to the nucleus itself, not a rearrangement of atoms or electrons.
A nucleus holding a very large number of protons and neutrons that is not stable, such as uranium or plutonium. Only nuclei of this kind undergo fission; small stable nuclei do not.
Fission that happens on its own, without the nucleus being struck by anything. It is rare, which is why fission fuel does not simply split apart by itself while it is in storage.
Usually, for fission to occur the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron. Neutrons are uncharged, so they are not repelled as they approach the nucleus.
What a fission event produces: two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size, together with two or three neutrons and gamma rays.
Energy is released by the fission reaction. It appears as the kinetic energy of the products and as the gamma radiation emitted.
Kinetic energy of the fission products
All of the fission products have kinetic energy: the two smaller nuclei and the two or three neutrons all move away from the split at speed.
The neutrons released by one fission may go on to be absorbed by other unstable nuclei, causing those nuclei to undergo fission and release further neutrons in turn.
The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released, so that the rate of fission and the energy output stay steady.
A chain reaction in which the number of fissions grows very rapidly. The explosion caused by a nuclear weapon is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction.
The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.
Mass converted into the energy of radiation
In fusion some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation, so the heavier nucleus formed has less mass than the two light nuclei had between them.
A quantity that has magnitude only. A scalar is fully described by a size and a unit, with no direction attached to it. Mass, speed, distance, energy and time are scalars.
A quantity that has magnitude and an associated direction. A vector is only fully described when both are given. Force, weight, velocity, displacement and acceleration are vectors.

The representation of a vector quantity by an arrow drawn on a diagram. The length of the arrow represents the magnitude of the vector, and the direction the arrow points represents the direction of the vector quantity.

A push or pull that acts on an object due to the interaction with another object. A force is not something an object stores or owns; it exists only while two objects interact, and it is measured in newtons.
A force between two objects that are physically touching. Friction, air resistance, tension and the normal contact force are contact forces.
A force between two objects that are physically separated. Gravitational force, electrostatic force and magnetic force are non-contact forces.
A contact force that acts between two surfaces that are touching, acting along the surfaces and opposing the relative motion, or attempted motion, between them.
A contact force acting on an object moving through air. The object is physically touching the particles of the air, which is why it is classed as a contact force.
A contact force transmitted along a stretched rope, string, cable or spring, pulling on the objects attached at each end of it.
The contact force exerted by a surface on an object that is touching it, acting at right angles (normal) to that surface.
A non-contact force of attraction between two objects that have mass. It acts even though the objects are physically separated, for example between the Earth and an object above its surface.
A non-contact force between electrically charged objects. Like charges repel and opposite charges attract, and the force acts across the space between the charged objects.
A non-contact force between magnets, or between a magnet and a magnetic material, which acts across the gap between them without the objects touching.
The two forces produced when two objects interact. Each object exerts a force on the other, the two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, and each force acts on a different object.

The force acting on an object due to gravity, measured in newtons, N. Close to the Earth it is due to the gravitational field around the Earth, and it is calculated from weight = mass × gravitational field strength.

The quantity, symbol g, measured in newtons per kilogram, N/kg, that describes the strength of a gravitational field at a point. The weight of an object depends on the gravitational field strength at the point where the object is.

The quantity of matter in an object, symbol m, measured in kilograms, kg. Mass is a scalar quantity and it does not change when the object is moved to a place with a different gravitational field strength.

The single point at which the weight of an object may be considered to act. Treating the weight as one force acting at this point allows an object to be handled as though all of its mass were concentrated there.

A relationship in which one quantity is a fixed multiple of another, so that multiplying one by a number multiplies the other by the same number, and a graph of one against the other is a straight line through the origin. The weight of an object and the mass of an object are directly proportional.
A calibrated spring-balance used to measure weight in newtons. The spring extends more as the force pulling on it increases, and the scale is marked so that the reading gives the weight directly.
The single force that has the same effect as all of the original forces acting on an object together. A number of forces acting on an object may always be replaced by this one force.

A diagram showing a single isolated object or system on its own, with every force acting on that object drawn as an arrow from it. It is used to describe qualitatively how several forces combine to give a resultant force.
Forces on an object that combine to give a resultant force of zero. The individual forces are still acting, but they have no overall effect on the motion of the object.
Replacing a single force by two component forces acting at right angles to each other. The two component forces together have the same effect as the single force they replace.
The situation in which the forces acting on an object are balanced, so the resultant force is zero. On a scale vector diagram the arrows representing the forces form a closed shape.

Work is done on an object when a force causes the object to move through a distance, that is when the force causes a displacement of the object. A force that produces no displacement does no work, however large the force is and however long it is applied for.
Distance moved along the line of action of the force

The distance s used in the work equation is the distance the object moves along the line of action of the force, not simply any distance it travels. Movement at right angles to the force contributes nothing to the work done by that force.

work done = force × distance (moved along the line of action of the force), written in symbols as W = F s, where work done, W, is in joules, J; force, F, is in newtons, N; and distance, s, is in metres.
The unit of work done and of energy. One joule of work is done when a force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre.

Force in newtons multiplied by distance in metres gives work in newton-metres. The newton-metre and the joule are the same size of unit: 1 joule = 1 newton-metre, so a value in N m converts to the identical number of J.
Energy transfer when work is done

Doing work is a way of transferring energy. When a force does work on an object, energy is transferred to that object, and the amount of energy transferred in joules is equal to the work done in joules.
When an object moves against frictional forces, work is done against those forces. The energy transferred is not lost: it raises the temperature of the object rather than making it move faster.

Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object, so surfaces such as brake blocks, rubbed hands and dragged crates become warmer as they move.
A change in the shape of an object caused by forces acting on it. An object may be deformed by stretching it, by bending it or by compressing (squashing) it.
Making an object longer by pulling its ends apart. Examples include a rubber band pulled between two hands and a spring hanging from a stand with a weight on the end.
Making an object shorter by pushing its ends towards each other. Examples include the suspension spring of a parked car and a spring squashed between a hand and the bench.
Changing the shape of an object so that one side is stretched while the other side is compressed, for example a diving board pushed down at the free end while the fixed end is held.
Why more than one force is needed
To change the shape of a stationary object, more than one force must be applied. A single force would produce a resultant force, and the object would accelerate away instead of changing shape.
Deformation from which an object returns to its original shape and length once the deforming forces are removed.
Deformation after which an object does not return to its original shape and length when the deforming forces are removed; it stays permanently changed.
The increase in length of an object compared with its original, unloaded length. Extension = stretched length - original length.
Two quantities are directly proportional when a graph of one against the other is a straight line through the origin, so doubling one doubles the other.
The point beyond which the extension of an object is no longer directly proportional to the force applied. Up to this point the force-extension graph is a straight line through the origin.
The relationship between the force applied to an elastic object and its extension, written as F = k e. It holds up to the limit of proportionality.
The force applied to the spring, measured in newtons, N. For a spring hanging from a stand with masses on it, this force is the weight of the masses.
A measure of the stiffness of a spring: the force needed per metre of extension, measured in newtons per metre, N/m. A stiffer spring has a larger spring constant.
The extension used in F = k e, measured in metres, m. Lengths measured in centimetres or millimetres must be converted to metres before the equation is used.
The same relationship applies when an elastic object is compressed. In that case e stands for the compression of the object rather than its extension.
Work done and elastic potential energy

A force that stretches or compresses a spring does work, and elastic potential energy is stored in the spring. Provided the spring is not inelastically deformed, the work done and the energy stored are equal.
A linear force-extension relationship gives a straight-line graph, so equal increases in force give equal increases in extension. A non-linear relationship gives a curve.
For a linear region, plotting force on the vertical axis against extension on the horizontal axis gives a straight line whose gradient is the spring constant, k.
The energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring, E_e = 1/2 k e^2, valid up to the limit of proportionality. Energy is in joules, J.
When a stretched or compressed spring is released, the elastic potential energy stored in it is transferred to other stores, for example to the kinetic energy store of an object it pushes.

An investigation of the relationship between force and extension for a spring: hang the spring from a stand, add known weights one at a time, and measure the length after each weight so that the extension can be found.
AT 1 and AT 2 in this practical
AT 1 is the use of apparatus to make length measurements; AT 2 is the safe use of apparatus to measure force. Both are used when a ruler and known weights are used on a loaded spring.
Working scientifically and maths skills here
The practical develops skills such as tabulating results, plotting force against extension, drawing a line of best fit, finding a gradient and identifying anomalous results.

A force, or a system of forces, may cause an object to rotate instead of simply moving along a straight line. Rotation happens when the line of action of the force misses the fixed point about which the object can turn, so that the force acts at some perpendicular distance from that point.

The fixed point about which an object turns. A moment is always stated about a particular pivot: the same force can have a large moment about one pivot and no moment at all about another, because the perpendicular distance differs in each case.

The turning effect of a force is called the moment of the force. It measures how strongly a force tends to turn an object about a pivot, and it depends on both the size of the force and its perpendicular distance from the pivot.

The size of the moment is defined by the equation moment of a force = force × distance, written in symbols as M = F d. The two quantities multiply, so doubling either the force or the distance doubles the moment.
Quantities and units in M = F d

Moment of a force, M, is in newton-metres, Nm. Force, F, is in newtons, N. Distance, d, is in metres, m. A mass given in kilograms must first be converted to a weight in newtons, and a distance given in centimetres or millimetres must be converted to metres, before the equation is used.

In M = F d the distance d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force, in metres. It is not necessarily the length of the object, nor the distance measured along the object to the point where the force is applied; when the force acts at an angle to the object the perpendicular distance is shorter than that.
Line of action of a force

The straight line drawn through the point at which a force acts, along the direction of the force and extended in both directions. The distance d is measured from the pivot at right angles to this line. If the line of action passes through the pivot, d is zero and the moment is zero.

Every force acting on an object turns it about the pivot in one of two senses. A moment that would turn the object clockwise is called a clockwise moment; one that would turn it the other way is an anticlockwise moment. Moments acting in the same sense are added together.

If an object is balanced, the total clockwise moment about a pivot equals the total anticlockwise moment about that pivot. It is the moments that must match, not the forces and not the distances, so a small force far from the pivot can balance a large force close to it.
Finding an unknown force or distance

For a balanced object, writing total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment gives one equation that can be solved for a single unknown. To find a force, divide the known moment by that force's distance; to find a distance, divide the known moment by that force.

A rigid bar that turns about a pivot. A force applied at a large distance from the pivot produces a large moment, which is transmitted through the bar and can move a much larger load acting close to the pivot. The lever transmits the rotational effect of the force; it does not create energy.

Two or more toothed wheels meshed together. The teeth of one wheel push on the teeth of the next, transmitting the rotational effect from one wheel to the other. Meshed gears turn in opposite senses, and a larger driven gear turns more slowly than the smaller driving gear but with a larger moment.
Everyday examples of forces causing rotation

Pushing the edge of a door so that it swings on its hinges, pressing a bicycle pedal so that the crank turns about the axle, and pulling on a spanner so that a nut turns are all cases in which a force applied at a distance from a pivot causes rotation.
