pressure-and-pressure-differences-in-flu.d: Pressure and pressure differences in fluids (physics only)
terms: A substance that can flow. A fluid can be either a liquid or a gas, so gases as well as liquids exert pressure on the surfaces they touch.
The force acting normal to a surface divided by the area of that surface. Pressure is measured in pascals, Pa.
At right angles to the surface. The pressure in a fluid causes a force normal to any surface the fluid is in contact with, whatever the angle of that surface.
The unit of pressure. One pascal is one newton acting normal to each square metre of surface, so 1 Pa = 1 N/m².
Pressure at the surface of a fluid
Calculated with pressure = (force normal to a surface)/(area of that surface), that is p = F/A, with F in newtons and A in metres squared.
The area of the surface over which the normal force is spread. For a fixed force, a larger area of contact gives a smaller pressure.
Pressure due to a column of liquid
Calculated with pressure = height of the column × density of the liquid × gravitational field strength, that is p = h ρ g.
The mass of a material per unit volume, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³. A denser liquid gives a greater pressure at the same depth.
The vertical height of liquid above the point of interest, in metres, m. It is the height of liquid above the point, not the width of the container.
The force of gravity on each kilogram of mass, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg. Its value is given in any calculation in this topic.
The extra pressure between two points in a liquid, found from the difference in height of the two points: Δp = Δh ρ g.
The resultant upward force on a partially or totally submerged object, caused by the pressure on its bottom surface being greater than the pressure on its top surface.
An object floats when the upthrust can balance its weight. An object whose density is less than the density of the liquid floats; a denser object sinks.
A thin layer of air round the Earth, thin compared with the size of the Earth, which gets less dense with increasing altitude.
The pressure caused by air molecules colliding with a surface. It comes from the weight of the air above that surface.
Height above ground level. As altitude increases there is less air above a surface, so atmospheric pressure decreases.
Distance is how far an object moves along the path it actually travels. It does not involve direction, so it is a scalar quantity: a magnitude and a unit fully describe it, for example 450 m.

Displacement is the distance an object moves measured in a straight line from the start point to the finish point, together with the direction of that straight line. It is quoted as a magnitude and a direction, for example 450 m due east.
A scalar quantity has magnitude only. Distance and speed are scalars: stating the number and the unit says everything there is to say about them.
A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction. Displacement and velocity are vectors: two vectors of the same size pointing different ways are different quantities.
Speed is how fast an object is moving. It does not involve direction, so speed is a scalar quantity, measured in metres per second, m/s.
The specification gives typical values that may be taken as: walking about 1.5 m/s, running about 3 m/s and cycling about 6 m/s. These are estimates to be recalled and used, not exact figures.

Students should also be able to recall typical speeds for different types of transportation system, for example a car on a motorway at roughly 30 m/s, a train at roughly 50 m/s and an aeroplane at roughly 250 m/s.
The speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle depends on many factors including age, terrain, fitness and the distance travelled.

The speed of a moving object is rarely constant: when people walk, run or travel in a car their speed changes constantly. It is not only moving objects that have varying speed, because the speed of sound and the speed of the wind also vary.
A typical value for the speed of sound in air is 330 m/s. The actual value varies, for example with the temperature of the air.
Speed is found by measuring a distance, for example with a ruler, tape measure or trundle wheel, measuring the time taken with a stopwatch or light gates, and then dividing the distance by the time.
For an object moving at constant speed the distance travelled in a specific time can be calculated using distance travelled = speed × time, written in symbols as [s = v t].
Quantities and units in [s = v t]
In s = v t the distance s is in metres, m; the speed v is in metres per second, m/s; and the time t is in seconds, s.
For non-uniform motion the average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken, including any time spent stationary.
The velocity of an object is its speed in a given direction, so velocity is a vector quantity. Two objects with equal speeds have different velocities if they move in different directions.
Distance and speed are scalars; displacement and velocity are the matching vector quantities. Each pair has the same unit, and the vector member of the pair also carries a direction.

An object moving in a circle at a steady rate has constant speed but changing velocity, because its direction of motion changes continuously. Examples include a car on a roundabout and a satellite in a circular orbit.
If an object moves along a straight line, the distance travelled can be represented by a distance-time graph, with time on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis.

The speed of an object can be calculated from the gradient of its distance-time graph: gradient is the change in distance divided by the change in time. A horizontal line has zero gradient, so the object is stationary.
Tangent to a distance-time graph (HT only)
If an object is accelerating, its speed at any particular time can be determined by drawing a tangent to the curve at that time and measuring the gradient of that tangent.
Students should be able to draw distance-time graphs from measurements, and extract and interpret lines and slopes, translating information between graphical and numerical form.
The average acceleration of an object can be calculated using acceleration = (change in velocity)/(time taken), written in symbols as [a = (∆v)/(t)].
Acceleration, a, is in metres per second squared, m/s^2; change in velocity, ∆ v, is in metres per second, m/s; and time, t, is in seconds, s.
An object that slows down is decelerating. Its acceleration has the opposite sign to its velocity, so for an object moving forwards the acceleration is negative.
Students should be able to estimate the magnitude of everyday accelerations, for example a family car pulling away at roughly 2 m/s^2 and an object falling freely at about 9.8 m/s^2.

The acceleration of an object can be calculated from the gradient of a velocity-time graph. Students should be able to draw velocity-time graphs from measurements and interpret lines and slopes to determine acceleration.
Area under a velocity-time graph (HT only)

The distance travelled by an object, or the displacement of an object, can be calculated from the area under a velocity-time graph, and students should be able to interpret enclosed areas to determine it.
Where the area under a velocity-time graph is not a simple triangle or rectangle, it can be measured, when appropriate, by counting squares and multiplying by the quantity one square represents.
The following equation applies to uniform acceleration: (final velocity)^2 - (initial velocity)^2 = 2 × acceleration × distance, written in symbols as [v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s].
Quantities and units in [v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s]
Final velocity v and initial velocity u are in metres per second, m/s; acceleration a is in metres per second squared, m/s^2; and distance s is in metres, m.
Near the Earth's surface any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s^2, whatever its mass.

An object falling through a fluid initially accelerates due to the force of gravity. As it speeds up the drag force grows until eventually the resultant force is zero and the object moves at its terminal velocity. Physics only: students should be able to draw and interpret velocity-time graphs for objects that reach terminal velocity and interpret the changing motion in terms of the forces acting.

If the resultant force acting on an object is zero, the object's velocity does not change: a stationary object remains stationary, and a moving object keeps moving at the same speed and in the same direction. It follows that the velocity of an object - its speed and/or its direction - will only change if a resultant force is acting on the object. The law says nothing about there being no forces; it is about the resultant of the forces being zero.
Zero resultant force on a stationary object

If the resultant force acting on an object is zero and the object is stationary, the object remains stationary. A book on a table has its weight pulling it down and the table pushing it up; these forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, so the resultant is zero and the book stays where it is. Forces are certainly acting - what is zero is their resultant.
Zero resultant force on a moving object

If the resultant force acting on an object is zero and the object is moving, the object continues to move at the same speed and in the same direction. So the object continues to move at the same velocity. No forward force is needed to keep an object moving; a force is only needed to change how it moves. On a frictionless surface an object given a push would carry on at that speed for ever.

When a vehicle travels at a steady speed the resistive forces balance the driving force. The engine's driving force is not larger than friction and air resistance - if it were, the resultant force would not be zero and the vehicle would be accelerating. The driving force is needed only to cancel the resistive forces, which is why a vehicle slows down as soon as the driving force is removed.

The velocity (speed and/or direction) of an object will only change if a resultant force is acting on the object. Because velocity includes direction, an object travelling round a bend at a constant speed has a changing velocity, so there must be a resultant force on it. A change of speed, a change of direction, or both, each require a resultant force.

To explain a motion, first decide whether the velocity is constant. If the object is stationary or moving with a uniform velocity, the forces on it must have a resultant of zero, so the opposing forces are equal in size - a skydiver at terminal velocity, a car at steady speed, a crate at rest. If the speed and/or the direction is changing, there must be a resultant force, and it acts in the direction of the change: forwards for a car speeding up, backwards for a train braking, towards the centre for a vehicle turning a corner.

The tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion is called inertia. Inertia is a tendency, not a force: nothing pushes a moving object along, it simply keeps moving because no resultant force is changing its velocity. Inertia is why a passenger continues to move forwards when a bus brakes sharply.

The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force acting on the object, and inversely proportional to the mass of the object. Doubling the resultant force on a given object doubles its acceleration; doubling the mass while keeping the resultant force the same halves the acceleration. The acceleration is always in the same direction as the resultant force.

Newton's Second Law as an equation is resultant force = mass x acceleration, written F = m a. This is one of the equations that must be recalled and applied. The force in the equation is always the resultant force, not one of the individual forces: for a car with a driving force of 4800 N and resistive forces of 1800 N, the F to use is 3000 N.
Quantities and units in F = m a

In F = m a the quantities are: force, F, in newtons, N; mass, m, in kilograms, kg; acceleration, a, in metres per second squared, m/s². Masses given in grams must be converted to kilograms before use, and a mass must never be entered as a weight in newtons. Acceleration is in m/s², not m/s - m/s is a speed.

The equation can be rearranged to find whichever quantity is unknown: a = F / m to find an acceleration, and m = F / a to find a mass. Both rearrangements involve dividing, never multiplying. A resultant force of 60 N on a mass of 15 kg gives a = 60 / 15 = 4.0 m/s²; a resultant force of 60 N producing an acceleration of 4.0 m/s² implies a mass of 60 / 4.0 = 15 kg.

Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object. If two objects are acted on by the same resultant force, the one that changes velocity less readily - the one with the smaller acceleration - has the greater inertial mass. It is measured in kilograms, like any other mass.

Inertial mass is defined as the ratio of force over acceleration. In symbols this is m = F / a, which is simply Newton's Second Law rearranged. Because it is a force divided by an acceleration, its unit is N divided by m/s², which is the kilogram - so inertial mass is a mass, not a force.
Estimating speeds, accelerations and forces on the road

Sensible everyday figures let you estimate the forces involved in large accelerations for road transport. A typical urban speed is about 13 m/s (30 mph) and a motorway speed about 31 m/s (70 mph); a family car has a mass of the order of 1000 to 1500 kg. A car accelerating briskly from rest to 27 m/s in about 9 s has an acceleration of roughly 3 m/s², and emergency braking can reach around 10 m/s². Putting these into F = m a gives resultant forces of the order of several thousand newtons - thousands, not tens.

The symbol ~ placed before a value shows that the value is approximate: it is an estimate rather than an exact answer. Writing 'resultant force ~ 4000 N' means the force is about 4000 N, a figure obtained from rounded, typical values. An estimate should still be worked out properly from an equation and quoted to one or two significant figures; the symbol signals the precision of the answer, not carelessness in getting it.

A trolley on a runway is pulled by a string that passes over a pulley at the end of the bench to a hanging mass holder; the weight of the hanging masses provides the accelerating force. The acceleration is found from light gates and a data logger, or from a tape produced by a ticker timer. To vary the force while keeping the mass of the object constant, masses are moved from the trolley to the hanger rather than simply added to the hanger, so that the total mass being accelerated stays the same. Friction is compensated for by tilting the runway slightly until the trolley runs at a steady speed after a gentle push.

In the second investigation the hanging masses are left unchanged, so the accelerating force is constant, and extra masses are loaded onto the trolley to increase the mass of the object. The acceleration is measured again for each mass. The independent variable is the mass, the dependent variable is the acceleration, and the control variable is the force.

With the mass constant, a graph of acceleration against resultant force is a straight line through the origin, showing that acceleration is proportional to the resultant force. With the force constant, acceleration falls as mass rises and a graph of acceleration against mass is a curve, not a straight line; plotting acceleration against 1 / mass straightens it, showing that acceleration is inversely proportional to mass. Together the two results are Newton's Second Law.

Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite. The two forces are always the same size, however different the two objects are: in a collision between a car and a lorry, the car pushes on the lorry exactly as hard as the lorry pushes on the car. Neither force comes first - they exist together for as long as the interaction lasts.
Identifying a Newton's Third Law pair

The two forces of a third law pair are equal in size, opposite in direction, of the same type (both contact forces, or both gravitational, for example), and - crucially - they act on two different objects. Because they act on different objects they can never cancel each other out; only forces acting on the same object can be added to give a resultant.
Newton's Third Law in equilibrium situations

For a person standing still on the floor, the floor pushes up on the person and the person pushes down on the floor: equal, opposite, and acting on different objects, so this is a third law pair. The person's weight and the floor's upward push are a different matter - both act on the person, and they happen to be equal because the person is in equilibrium under Newton's First Law. In equilibrium the resultant force on each object is zero, and every interaction contributes a pair of equal and opposite forces.
Newton's First Law and Third Law compared

Balanced forces (First Law) and a third law pair (Third Law) are different ideas that are easily confused. Balanced forces act on the same single object, may be of different types, and are equal only because that object's velocity is not changing. A third law pair acts on two different objects, is always of the same type, and is always equal whether or not anything is in equilibrium.

The total distance a vehicle travels from the moment the driver sees a hazard to the moment the vehicle comes to rest. It is the sum of the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time (thinking distance) and the distance travelled under the braking force (braking distance): stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.

The distance the vehicle travels during the driver's reaction time, before the brakes are applied. The vehicle is still moving at its original speed throughout, so thinking distance = speed x reaction time. It is therefore directly proportional to speed: double the speed and the thinking distance doubles.

The distance the vehicle travels under the braking force, measured from the moment the brakes are applied to the moment the vehicle stops. It depends on the speed, the braking force, the road and weather conditions and the condition of the vehicle's brakes and tyres.
Effect of speed on stopping distance

For a given braking force the greater the speed of the vehicle, the greater the stopping distance. Both parts grow: the thinking distance grows in proportion to speed, and the braking distance grows more steeply still, because the work the brakes must do equals the kinetic energy of the vehicle, and kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed.

Reaction times vary from person to person. Typical values range from 0.2 s to 0.9 s. That spread matters on the road: at 13 m/s (about 30 mph) a reaction time of 0.2 s gives a thinking distance of about 2.6 m, while 0.9 s gives about 12 m from the same speed.
Factors affecting a driver's reaction time

A driver's reaction time can be affected by tiredness, drugs and alcohol. Each of these lengthens the reaction time, so at any given speed they lengthen the thinking distance and therefore the stopping distance. They do not change the braking distance.

Distractions may also affect a driver's ability to react - for example using a mobile phone, adjusting the radio or talking to passengers. Like tiredness, drugs and alcohol, a distraction acts on the reaction time and so on the thinking distance, leaving the braking distance unchanged.
Measuring reaction time: the ruler drop method

One student holds a ruler vertically with the zero mark between the open thumb and finger of a second student, then releases it without warning. The catcher closes their fingers as soon as they see it move. The distance the ruler falls is measured and converted into a time using a conversion chart, because the ruler is in free fall. A shorter fall means a shorter reaction time.
Measuring reaction time: computer methods and typical results

Reaction time can also be measured with a computer or tablet program in which the user clicks or taps as soon as a shape appears or a sound is played; the machine times the response itself, so the experimenter's own reaction time cannot creep into the result. Typical classroom results are about 0.2 s to 0.3 s, at the fast end of the 0.2 s to 0.9 s range.

Repeat the test several times for each student, identify any clearly anomalous result and leave it out, then calculate a mean of the rest. Keep everything else the same - the same ruler, the same starting gap between the fingers, no countdown before the drop - so that any difference between students is due to reaction time and not to the way the test was run.
Judging the effect of a factor on thinking distance from data

To evaluate how a factor such as tiredness, alcohol or a phone call affects thinking distance, compare thinking distances measured at the same speed. Dividing a thinking distance by the speed converts it back to a reaction time, which allows results taken at different speeds to be compared fairly.

The braking distance of a vehicle can be affected by adverse road and weather conditions. Adverse road conditions include wet or icy conditions. They reduce the grip between the tyres and the road, so the vehicle travels further before it stops. They have no effect on the driver's reaction time, so the thinking distance is unchanged.

Braking distance is also increased by poor condition of the vehicle. Poor condition of the vehicle is limited to the vehicle's brakes or tyres - for example worn brake pads that cannot produce the full braking force, or tyres with too little tread to clear water from the road surface.
Estimating stopping distance at typical speeds

Estimate the thinking distance from thinking distance = speed x reaction time, using a reaction time of about 0.7 s for an alert driver. Estimate the braking distance from the braking deceleration using v2 - u2 = 2 a s, which is given in the exam; a typical family car on a dry road decelerates at about 6.5 m/s2. At 13 m/s (about 30 mph) that gives roughly 9 m + 13 m = 22 m, and at 27 m/s (about 60 mph) roughly 19 m + 56 m = 75 m.

Plotted against speed, thinking distance is a straight line through the origin, while braking distance is a curve that rises ever more steeply. The total stopping distance curve therefore also becomes steeper as speed increases. When two vehicles are plotted together, the one whose line lies higher needs the greater distance to stop at every speed.
Work done by the braking friction force

When a force is applied to the brakes of a vehicle, work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle and the temperature of the brakes increases. Energy is transferred from the kinetic store of the vehicle to the thermal store of the brakes; none of it is destroyed.

The greater the speed of a vehicle the greater the braking force needed to stop the vehicle in a certain distance. The work done by the brakes is the braking force multiplied by the braking distance, and it must equal the kinetic energy of the vehicle; so if the distance is fixed, a vehicle with more kinetic energy needs a larger force.
Braking force, deceleration and its dangers

The greater the braking force the greater the deceleration of the vehicle. Large decelerations may lead to brakes overheating and/or loss of control. Overheated brakes become less effective, and a vehicle that skids can no longer be steered.
Estimating the force in a deceleration

(HT only) Estimate the deceleration first, either from acceleration = change in velocity / time taken, or from v2 - u2 = 2 a s, which is given in the exam. Then use resultant force = mass x acceleration, F = m a, which must be recalled. A typical family car has a mass of about 1000 kg to 1500 kg, so an emergency stop at about 6.5 m/s2 needs a braking force of roughly 7000 N to 10 000 N.

Because stopping distance rises with speed, and rises further in wet or icy conditions or with worn brakes or tyres, safe driving means leaving a gap big enough to cover the whole stopping distance and cutting speed when conditions are poor. Speed limits, minimum tyre tread depths and brake testing all exist because those factors change how far a vehicle needs in order to stop.

A property of a moving object. The specification defines momentum by an equation: momentum is the object's mass multiplied by its velocity. Because velocity appears in the definition, an object has momentum only while it is moving — a stationary object has zero momentum however large its mass is.

The word equation that defines momentum. In the AQA list of equations this is one that students are required to recall, so it must be learned rather than looked up. Both quantities on the right must be in SI units before it is used: mass in kilograms and velocity in metres per second.

The symbol form of the momentum equation: p is momentum, m is mass and v is velocity. It rearranges to m = p / v and to v = p / m, so any one of the three quantities can be found when the other two are known.

Momentum, p, in kilograms metre per second, kg m/s. The unit follows directly from the equation: kilograms (mass) multiplied by metres per second (velocity). It is not the newton, which is the unit of force, and not the joule, which is the unit of energy.

Mass, m, in kilograms, kg. A mass given in grams must be converted to kilograms before p = m v is used — divide by 1000. A value in newtons is a weight, not a mass, and cannot be substituted into the equation.
Velocity, v, in metres per second, m/s. Velocity is the speed of the object in a given direction, so the number substituted into p = m v carries a direction with it.

Because momentum is mass multiplied by velocity, and velocity has a direction, momentum has a direction too. For objects moving along one line, choose one direction as positive; anything moving the other way then has a negative velocity and so a negative momentum. Two objects of equal mass moving towards each other at the same speed have momenta that cancel to zero.

A system that nothing enters and nothing leaves, and on which no external force acts. Conservation of momentum is stated by the specification for a closed system, so the two colliding trolleys, or the two skaters, must be considered together and treated as free from outside forces such as a push from a hand.

The momenta of all the objects in the system added together, with direction taken into account. An object moving in the negative direction contributes a negative amount, so the total can be smaller than either individual momentum, and can be zero.

In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after the event. This is called conservation of momentum. It is what makes an unknown velocity after a collision findable: total momentum after must equal the total worked out before.
Momentum as a model for an event

An event is anything that changes how the objects in a system are moving — most often a collision. Momentum is used as a model for such an event: individual objects gain or lose momentum, but the total for the closed system does not change, so any momentum one object loses has been transferred to the other.
Collision in which the objects join

When two objects collide and move off together, they afterwards have one combined mass and one shared velocity. Total momentum before is worked out from the separate objects; total momentum after is the combined mass multiplied by that shared velocity, and the two totals are equal.

If two objects are stationary and then push each other apart, the total momentum before the event is zero, so the total afterwards must also be zero. The two objects therefore move in opposite directions with momenta of equal size — which means the lighter object moves off with the greater speed.

When a force acts on an object that is moving, or able to move, a change in momentum occurs. The change is written m ∆v, where ∆v is the change in velocity — the final velocity minus the initial velocity — not the final velocity itself. A car of mass 1200 kg slowing from 20 m/s to rest has a change in momentum of 1200 × 20 = 24 000 kg m/s.

Force equals the change in momentum divided by the time taken for that change. Force, F, in newtons, N; m ∆v is the change in momentum in kg m/s; ∆t is the time in seconds, s. This equation is provided on the AQA Physics equation sheet, so it does not have to be recalled, but it does have to be selected and used correctly.
Force as the rate of change of momentum

'Rate of change of momentum' means the change in momentum divided by the time taken, not the total momentum divided by the time. Force equals that rate: for one fixed change in momentum, the longer the change takes, the smaller the force.
Combining F = m × a with a = (v − u)/t

Substituting the acceleration equation into the force equation gives F = m(v − u)/t. Since (v − u) is the change in velocity, ∆v, and t is the time for that change, ∆t, this is F = (m ∆v)/(∆t). The momentum equation is not a new law — it is Newton's Second Law written in terms of momentum.
Increasing the time of a collision

In a crash or a landing, the change in momentum is fixed by how fast the person was going and by their mass — it cannot be reduced by the safety feature. What the safety feature changes is ∆t. Increasing the time taken for the momentum to fall to zero reduces m ∆v ÷ ∆t, and so reduces the force on the person.

Air bags, seat belts, gymnasium crash mats, cycle helmets and cushioned surfaces for playgrounds all work the same way: they deform, stretch or squash, so the person is brought to rest over a longer time. The rate of change of momentum is smaller, so the force on the person is smaller.

Force, mass, velocity and acceleration are linked through F = m a, a = (v − u)/t and F = (m ∆v)/(∆t). Holding the change in momentum fixed and making the time five times longer makes the force five times smaller; holding the time fixed and doubling the change in velocity doubles the force. Explaining a safety feature means saying which quantity is held fixed and which one has been changed.

waves-in-air-fluids-and-solids-transvers.d: Waves in air, fluids and solids — part 4.6.1.1
terms: A travelling oscillation that carries energy from one place to another without the material it passes through being carried along. Waves may be either transverse or longitudinal.
A wave in which the oscillations are at right angles (perpendicular) to the direction in which the wave travels.
A wave in which the oscillations are along (parallel to) the direction in which the wave travels.
The standard example of a transverse wave. The surface of the water oscillates up and down while the ripple itself travels outwards across the surface, at right angles to that up-and-down movement.
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are pushed closer together than normal, so the density and the pressure there are higher than normal.
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are spread further apart than normal, so the density and the pressure there are lower than normal.
A longitudinal wave. A vibrating source such as a loudspeaker cone pushes and pulls the air next to it, sending a series of compressions and rarefactions travelling out through the air.
Each particle of the material vibrates to and fro about one position and returns to it. The particle does not travel along with the wave; it only passes the disturbance on to its neighbours.
Direction of travel of the wave

The direction in which the wave itself moves away from the source. A wave is classified as transverse or longitudinal by comparing the direction of the oscillations with this direction, not with 'up and down' or 'sideways'.

A cork or polystyrene ball floating in a ripple tank bobs up and down in the same place as ripples pass beneath it, instead of being carried to the far side. The ripple crosses the tank; the water does not.

A loudspeaker can be heard right across a room, yet no draught of air arrives with the sound and the air by the loudspeaker is never used up. The sound wave crosses the room; the air itself only vibrates in place.

waves-in-air-fluids-and-solids-propertie.d: Waves in air, fluids and solids — part 4.6.1.2
terms: Any wave, transverse or longitudinal, is described using four quantities: amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period. Amplitude describes the size of the oscillation; wavelength describes how long one complete wave is; frequency and period describe its timing and are two ways of stating the same information, since T = 1/f. Wave speed is a further quantity, but it is calculated from frequency and wavelength rather than being one of the four descriptive quantities.

The amplitude of a wave is the maximum displacement of a point on a wave away from its undisturbed position. It is measured from the undisturbed line up to a crest, or from the undisturbed line down to a trough — never from a trough all the way up to a crest, which is twice the amplitude. Amplitude is a distance and is read on the displacement axis of a wave diagram.

The undisturbed position is where a point in the medium would sit if no wave were passing — its rest position. On a wave diagram it is the centre line about which the wave oscillates, and it is the line from which amplitude is measured. Displacement is measured from this line, so a point at the undisturbed position has zero displacement even though the wave is still passing.

The wavelength of a wave is the distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave. Crest to the next crest, trough to the next trough, or any point to the matching point one wave later all give the same distance. Wavelength is given the symbol λ and measured in metres, m. A crest to the neighbouring trough is only half a wavelength.

The frequency of a wave is the number of waves passing a point each second. It is a counting rate — not a speed, and not a count of how many waves happen to be drawn on a diagram. Frequency is given the symbol f and measured in hertz, Hz, where 1 Hz means one complete wave passing each second.

The period of a wave is the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point, and it is the reciprocal of the frequency: period = (1)/(frequency). A high frequency therefore means a short period. A wave of frequency 8 Hz has a period of 1/8 = 0.125 s, because eight waves share each second.

The specification states the relationship as period = (1)/(frequency), in symbols [T = 1/f]. Because the two quantities are reciprocals, the relationship rearranges to f = 1/T, so either can be found from the other. A period of 0.004 s gives f = 1/0.004 = 250 Hz. Period and frequency are never equal in value unless both are 1.

The specification gives period, T, in seconds, s. Period is a time, so its unit is the second — the same unit as any other time interval. Periods of waves are often small fractions of a second, so answers such as 0.004 s are normal and should not be rounded to zero or converted into hertz.

The specification gives frequency, f, in hertz, Hz. One hertz is one complete wave passing a point each second. Larger frequencies are often quoted in kilohertz, kHz, or megahertz, MHz: 1 kHz = 1000 Hz and 1 MHz = 1 000 000 Hz, so a frequency in kHz is multiplied by 1000 to convert it into hertz before it is used in the wave equation.

The wave speed is the speed at which the energy is transferred (or the wave moves) through the medium. It is not the speed of the particles of the medium, which only oscillate about their undisturbed positions and are not carried along with the wave. Wave speed is given the symbol v and measured in metres per second, m/s.
All waves obey the wave equation

All waves obey the wave equation: it holds for transverse and longitudinal waves alike, and for waves in air, in fluids and in solids. Sound, ripples on water, waves on a string and electromagnetic waves are all covered by the same relationship, so a single equation links speed, frequency and wavelength for every wave met in this course.

The wave equation is wave speed = frequency × wavelength, in symbols [v = f λ]. It rearranges to f = v/λ and to λ = v/f. Because the speed is a product of the other two, a wave that keeps the same speed has a wavelength that falls as its frequency rises. Substituting f in Hz and λ in m always gives v in m/s.

The specification gives wave speed, v, in metres per second, m/s; frequency, f, in hertz, Hz; and wavelength, λ, in metres, m. The equation only produces a speed in m/s if the wavelength is entered in metres and the frequency in hertz, so a wavelength quoted in centimetres or millimetres must be converted first, and a frequency in kilohertz must be multiplied by 1000.
Reading amplitude and wavelength from a diagram

On a displacement–distance graph, amplitude is read vertically on the displacement axis, from the undisturbed centre line to a crest or trough, while wavelength is read horizontally on the distance axis, from one point to the equivalent point on the next wave. The two quantities are therefore measured on different axes, and confusing the axes is the commonest error when identifying them from a given diagram.
Measuring the speed of sound in air

A workable method is to stand a measured distance from a large reflecting wall, clap, and time the echo returning; the sound has travelled twice the distance to the wall, so wave speed = (2 × distance) ÷ time. Distances of many tens of metres, and timings taken over several claps, are used so that human reaction time is small compared with the time being measured. An alternative method uses two microphones a measured distance apart connected to an electronic timer.
Measuring the speed of ripples on a water surface

A ripple tank with a vibrating dipper produces ripples whose pattern is projected onto a screen below. The frequency is read from the signal generator driving the dipper, and the wavelength is measured with a ruler laid against the projected pattern, ideally across ten wavelengths which are then divided by ten. The wave speed is then found from v = f λ. A stroboscope or a video frame freezes the moving pattern so that it can be measured.
Sound passing from one medium to another

When a sound wave crosses from one medium into another, its frequency is fixed by the vibrating source and does not change. The wave speed does change, because it depends on the medium — sound travels faster in water, and faster still in solids, than in air. Since v = f λ and f is fixed, the wavelength must change in the same proportion as the speed: a faster medium gives a longer wavelength.

In this practical, observations are made to identify the suitability of apparatus for measuring the frequency, wavelength and speed of waves in a ripple tank and of waves in a solid, and appropriate measurements are taken. Typical judgements include using a ruler on the projected pattern rather than a stopwatch on a single ripple, reading the frequency from the signal generator, and measuring across ten wavelengths on a stretched string before dividing by ten.

waves-in-air-fluids-and-solids-reflectio.d: Waves in air, fluids and solids — part 4.6.1.3
terms: The surface where one material ends and a different material begins, such as air and glass, air and water, or air and a brick wall. When a wave reaches a boundary it can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted.
When a wave meets the boundary between two different materials and is sent back into the material it came from. Reflection happens to all waves, not only to light, and not only at mirrors.

A construction line drawn at 90° to the surface at the point where the ray meets it. It is drawn as a dashed line and is the line from which the angles of incidence and reflection are always measured.
Angle of incidence and angle of reflection
The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal. The angle of reflection is the angle between the reflected ray and the normal. Neither is measured from the surface.
For a wave reflected at a surface, the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. The incident ray and the reflected ray lie on opposite sides of the normal.

A diagram showing the surface, the incident ray with an arrow towards the point of incidence, the dashed normal at 90° to the surface at that point, and the reflected ray with an arrow away from it, drawn so that the marked angle of reflection equals the marked angle of incidence.

When a wave crosses the boundary and carries on travelling through the second material. The wave travels at a different speed in the new material, so unless it meets the boundary along the normal it also changes direction.

When a wave is taken in by the material at the boundary and does not continue as a wave. The energy carried by the wave is transferred to the energy stores of the absorbing material, usually its thermal store, so the material warms up.

The change of direction of a transmitted wave at a boundary, caused by the change in the speed of the wave. Light entering glass or perspex from air slows down and bends towards the normal; on leaving into air it speeds up and bends away from the normal.

At a real boundary all three effects usually happen together in different proportions. A window reflects a faint image, transmits most of the light and absorbs a little; a black matt surface absorbs most of the light and warms up; a hard wall reflects sound to give an echo, while curtains and carpet absorb sound so echoes die away.
Reflection by different types of surface

In the required practical, a smooth shiny surface such as a plane mirror sends a narrow ray back as one clear reflected ray, while a rough surface such as white paper or crumpled foil scatters the light in many directions. Each individual ray still obeys the law of reflection; on a rough surface the normals point in many different directions.

Place the surface on a sheet of paper and draw round it. Shine a narrow ray from a ray box with a single slit at the surface. Mark the incident ray and the reflected ray with two dots each, well apart. Remove the surface, join the dots, draw the normal at 90° to the surface at the point of incidence, and measure the angles of incidence and reflection with a protractor. Repeat for different types of surface.

Place a transparent block on paper and draw round it. Shine a narrow ray into one face at a chosen angle of incidence and mark the ray going in and the ray coming out. Remove the block, join the marks to show the path inside, draw the normal at the point where the ray entered, and measure the angle of refraction. Repeat with blocks of different substances using the same angle of incidence each time, and compare how much each one bends the ray.
AT 4 and AT 8 in this practical

Both of these apparatus and techniques statements are about observing how waves interact with matter. They are met here by using a ray box or lamp with a single narrow slit, transparent blocks and different surfaces to observe how light is reflected and refracted, and by using a protractor and sharp pencil to record the angles accurately.
Working scientifically and maths skills in this practical

The investigation gives opportunities to identify and control variables, such as keeping the angle of incidence the same when different substances are compared, to measure angles to the nearest degree, to repeat readings and identify anomalies, and to plot and interpret a graph of angle of refraction against angle of incidence.

waves-in-air-fluids-and-solids-part-4-6-.d: Waves in air, fluids and solids — part 4.6.1.4
terms: Sound wave travelling through a solid

A sound wave can travel through a solid, not only through air. As it passes, it causes vibrations in the solid itself: the particles of the solid are made to vibrate about their fixed positions and pass the disturbance on to their neighbours, so the wave is carried through the material.
A thin solid membrane inside the ear. A sound wave arriving at the ear drum makes it vibrate, so the ear drum is the point at which a sound wave in air is converted into vibrations of a solid.

Within the ear, sound waves cause the ear drum and other parts to vibrate, and it is this vibration that causes the sensation of sound. If the vibration is not produced, there is no sensation of sound.

The conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids works only over a limited frequency range: the solid parts involved can be made to vibrate by some frequencies but not by others. Outside that range the wave disturbance is not converted into vibration of the solid.

Because the ear drum and other parts of the ear only convert sound to vibration over a limited frequency range, human hearing has both an upper and a lower frequency limit. The range of normal human hearing is from 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), the number of waves passing a point each second. One kilohertz (1 kHz) is 1000 Hz, so the upper limit of normal human hearing, 20 kHz, is the same as 20 000 Hz.
Converting sound waves into vibrations of a solid

A process in which a sound wave in air arrives at a solid and makes that solid vibrate. Examples: sound waves striking the ear drum and making it vibrate; sound waves striking the diaphragm of a microphone and making it vibrate.
Converting vibrations of a solid into sound waves

The reverse process, in which a vibrating solid disturbs the air next to it and sends out a sound wave. Examples: the cone of a loudspeaker vibrating and producing sound waves in the air; a struck solid object vibrating and producing a sound.

waves-in-air-fluids-and-solids-part-4-6-.d: Waves in air, fluids and solids — part 4.6.1.5
terms: Sound waves with a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans. Ultrasound is ordinary sound — a longitudinal wave needing a medium to travel through — and differs from audible sound only in having too high a frequency for the human ear to detect.
The highest frequency a human ear can detect. This specification gives the normal range of human hearing as 20 Hz to 20 kHz, so any sound wave with a frequency above about 20 000 Hz is ultrasound.

The surface where one material meets a different material, such as the surface between two tissues in the body, between metal and the air inside a crack, or between water and the sea bed. A boundary matters because the wave behaves differently on each side of it — it travels at a different speed and is absorbed by a different amount.

When ultrasound waves meet a boundary between two different media they are partially reflected: part of the wave is reflected back towards the detector and the rest carries on into the second medium. Because the reflection is only partial, the transmitted part can go on to reflect from deeper boundaries, so several boundaries can be found from a single pulse.
Finding a distance from the time of a reflection

The time taken for a reflection to reach a detector is used to work out how far away the boundary is. The distance the pulse travels is found from distance travelled = speed × time, using the speed of the wave in that medium. Because the pulse travels to the boundary and back, the distance to the boundary is half the distance the pulse has travelled.

A use of ultrasound in which a pulse is sent into the body and the reflections from the boundaries between different tissues are timed. Each boundary returns its reflection after a different time, so the depths of the boundaries can be found and built into an image of a structure that cannot be seen directly.

A use of ultrasound in which a pulse is sent into a manufactured object, such as a metal casting or a weld. A crack or void inside the object is a boundary between two different media, so it partially reflects the pulse; a reflection arriving earlier than the reflection from the far side shows that a flaw lies inside the object.

The transfer of energy from a wave to the material it is passing through, which reduces the energy the wave carries. Different types of wave are absorbed by different amounts in the same material, so a wave that is only weakly absorbed by a material can be used to explore what lies beyond it, while a strongly absorbed wave cannot.
Velocity of a wave in a medium

The speed at which a wave travels through a particular material. The same wave travels at different speeds in different solids and liquids, and different types of wave travel at different speeds through the same material. A change of speed at a boundary is what makes the boundary reflect part of the wave, and the speed must be known before a time can be turned into a distance.
Waves produced by earthquakes, which travel through the Earth and are picked up by detectors at the surface. They are of two kinds, P-waves and S-waves.
A longitudinal seismic wave. P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids, so their speed changes when they cross from one part of the Earth's interior into another.
A transverse seismic wave. S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, so any region of the Earth's interior that S-waves fail to cross is evidence that the material there is liquid.

P-waves and S-waves provide evidence for the structure and size of the Earth's core. Detectors on the far side of the Earth from an earthquake receive no S-waves, which is evidence that part of the core is liquid; P-waves do arrive, but their speed changes where they cross into and out of the core, which alters the paths they follow and gives evidence about the size of the core and the structure within it.

The use of high frequency sound waves to detect objects in deep water and to measure water depth. A pulse is sent down from a ship, and the time for the echo to return from the sea bed or from an object is used to find how far away it is.

Structures that cannot be seen or reached — the inside of a body, a flaw inside a solid casting, the sea bed under deep water, the interior of the Earth. Waves reach these structures and return, so their differences in velocity, absorption and reflection allow the structures to be detected and explored indirectly. The study of seismic waves provided new evidence of exactly this kind, leading to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable.
Detection and exploration using differences between waves

Detection means finding that something is there; exploration means working out its size, depth or structure. Both rest on the same three differences: a wave travelling at a different velocity in the hidden material is partially reflected at its boundary, the time of that reflection gives the distance, and a wave that is weakly absorbed by the material in between is the one that can reach the structure and return.
A transverse wave that transfers energy from the source of the wave to an absorber. Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum, so they do not need a substance to travel through.
A wave in which the oscillations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer. All electromagnetic waves are transverse; sound waves, by contrast, are longitudinal.

The object or device that emits the electromagnetic wave and from which the energy is transferred away. Examples include the Sun, a lamp filament, a radio transmitter, the magnetron in a microwave oven and an X-ray tube.

The object that takes in the electromagnetic wave and receives the energy it carries. Examples include skin warmed by the Sun, water in food in a microwave oven, a solar cell, a receiving aerial and the retina of an eye.

Electromagnetic waves carry energy away from a source and deliver it to an absorber; no matter travels from the source to the absorber. Evidence of the transfer is a change in the absorber, such as a rise in temperature, a current in an aerial or a chemical change in the skin.

The electromagnetic spectrum runs without gaps from the longest wavelengths to the shortest. The seven named groups are convenient labels for regions of one unbroken spectrum, not seven separate kinds of wave, and the boundaries between them are not sharp.
A space containing no matter. Electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum, which is why light, infrared and ultraviolet from the Sun reach the Earth across empty space.

All types of electromagnetic wave travel at the same velocity through a vacuum (space) or air. Radio waves, visible light and gamma rays from the same event therefore arrive at the same time; the groups differ in wavelength and frequency, not in speed.

The distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the next wave. Wavelength is one of the two properties used to group the electromagnetic spectrum; radio waves have the longest wavelengths and gamma rays the shortest.

The number of waves passing a point each second. Frequency is the other property used to group the spectrum. Across the spectrum, going from long to short wavelength is the same as going from low to high frequency.
Going from long to short wavelength (or from low to high frequency) the groups are: radio, microwave, infrared, visible light (red to violet), ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.

The group of the electromagnetic spectrum that lies between infrared and ultraviolet. Within visible light, going from long to short wavelength runs from red to violet, so red has the longest wavelength of the visible colours and violet the shortest.
Limited detection range of the eye

Our eyes only detect visible light, so they detect a limited range of electromagnetic waves. Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays all reach us unseen and need instruments, not eyes, to detect them.
The waves that form the electromagnetic spectrum are grouped in terms of their wavelength and their frequency — not in terms of their speed, their amplitude or how they are made.

When a wave meets a substance and its energy is transferred into that substance rather than continuing through it. The wave does not emerge on the far side, and the internal energy of the substance rises.
When a wave passes through a substance and continues on the other side of it. A substance that transmits a wave allows it through with little of its energy being absorbed.
When a wave meets a boundary and is sent back into the substance it came from, instead of passing into the second substance.

The change in direction of a wave as it crosses the boundary between two different substances at an angle to the normal. A ray diagram shows it as the incident ray and the refracted ray making different angles with the normal.
Variation of these effects with wavelength

How a substance behaves towards electromagnetic waves is not a single fixed property of that substance. The same substance may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect waves of different wavelengths in different ways: glass transmits visible light but absorbs much of the ultraviolet reaching it, and brick transmits radio waves but not visible light.
Difference in velocity as the cause of refraction

Electromagnetic waves travel at different velocities in different substances. Some effects, refraction among them, are due to that difference in velocity: if the velocity of the wave is the same in both substances, no refraction occurs at the boundary between them.

A construction line drawn at right angles to the boundary at the point where the ray meets it, shown as a dashed line in a ray diagram. Every angle in a ray diagram is measured between a ray and the normal, never between a ray and the boundary.
Angle of incidence and angle of refraction
The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal. The angle of refraction is the angle between the refracted ray and the normal on the far side of the boundary.

A straight line with an arrow on it showing the direction in which the wave is travelling. A ray diagram of refraction shows the incident ray up to the boundary, the normal at that point, and the refracted ray continuing into the second medium.

Draw the boundary, then the normal as a dashed line where the incident ray meets it. A ray passing from air into glass or water bends towards the normal, so the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence. A ray passing from glass or water into air bends away from the normal. A ray that travels along the normal is not bent and carries straight on.

A line joining points on a wave that are all at the same point in their cycle, for example a line along a crest. Wave fronts are drawn at right angles to the direction in which the wave is travelling, and the distance between one wave front and the next is one wavelength.

When a wave front reaches the boundary at an angle, the end that crosses first changes speed first while the rest of the front is still travelling at the original speed. The front is therefore turned, and the direction of travel of the wave changes. In the medium in which the wave travels more slowly the wave fronts are drawn closer together, because the wave moves a shorter distance in each cycle; the frequency of the wave is unchanged.
Dependence of infrared absorption and emission on the surface

Every surface both absorbs and emits infrared radiation, but the amount depends on the nature of the surface. Matt, dark surfaces are the best absorbers and the best emitters of infrared radiation. Shiny, light-coloured surfaces are the poorest absorbers and the poorest emitters, and the best reflectors.

A sealed metal cube whose vertical faces carry different surfaces, typically matt black, matt white, shiny black and shiny silver. It is filled with hot water so that all four faces are at the same temperature, and an infrared detector held the same distance from each face in turn compares the radiation each surface emits.
Control variables in required practical activity 10

Only the nature of the surface may be changed. The distance between the surface and the detector or heater, the time for which readings are taken, the starting temperature, and the position and height of the detector must all be kept the same, or a difference in the readings cannot be attributed to the surface.

AT 1 covers the use of appropriate apparatus to make and record a range of measurements accurately. In this activity that means measuring distance with a ruler, time with a stopwatch, and temperature with a thermometer or infrared detector, and recording those readings to the resolution the instrument allows.

AT 4 covers making observations of the effects of the interaction of electromagnetic waves with matter. In this activity that means observing how infrared radiation interacts with surfaces of different nature — how much each surface absorbs when it faces a radiant heater, and how much each emits when it is hot.
WS and MS opportunities in this practical

The activity also gives opportunities to develop working scientifically skills, such as identifying control variables, judging the resolution and repeatability of measurements and evaluating the method, and mathematical skills, such as tabulating readings, calculating means and plotting temperature against time. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.

A repeated back-and-forth change of the current in a circuit, so that the charges move first one way and then the other, over and over. (HT only) Oscillations of this kind in an electrical circuit can produce radio waves.
(HT only) Radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits. The oscillating circuit is the source: the faster the oscillation, the higher the frequency of the radio wave produced.

(HT only) When radio waves are absorbed they may create an alternating current, so radio waves can themselves induce oscillations in an electrical circuit. Production and absorption are therefore two directions of the same link between radio waves and oscillating circuits.
Frequency of the induced alternating current

(HT only) The alternating current created when a radio wave is absorbed has the same frequency as the radio wave itself. A 200 kHz radio wave absorbed by a circuit induces an alternating current of 200 kHz.
Atoms and nuclei as sources of electromagnetic waves

Changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms can result in electromagnetic waves being generated or absorbed over a wide frequency range. The same atom can therefore be involved in emitting or absorbing radiation from very different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom. This origin, rather than any figure for frequency or wavelength, is what the specification uses to identify where gamma rays come from.

Radiation dose is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure of the body to radiation. It is not a count of the radiation itself: it combines how much radiation the body received with how damaging that type of radiation is.
The sievert is the unit in which radiation dose is measured. A dose quoted in sieverts tells you about the risk of harm from an exposure, so a larger number of sieverts means a greater risk of harm.

A smaller unit of radiation dose, used for the everyday doses people actually receive. 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), so to convert a dose in mSv to Sv you divide by 1000, and to convert Sv to mSv you multiply by 1000.
X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation. Being ionising is what makes them hazardous to human body tissue: they can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.
Ultraviolet waves can have hazardous effects on human body tissue: they can cause skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer.
A change to a gene caused by ionising radiation. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.

Using data you are given about radiation doses to compare exposures and comment on the risks and consequences. Doing this properly means converting all the doses to the same unit before comparing them, and stating conclusions as differences in risk rather than as certain outcomes.
Practical application of an electromagnetic wave

A use that is made of one part of the electromagnetic spectrum. The specification pairs each group with examples: radio waves with television and radio; microwaves with satellite communications and cooking food; infrared with electrical heaters, cooking food and infrared cameras; visible light with fibre optic communications; ultraviolet with energy efficient lamps and sun tanning; X-rays and gamma rays with medical imaging and treatments.
Television and radio programmes are broadcast as radio waves. A transmitter sends the signal out as radio waves and the aerial of a television set or radio receiver picks it up.

Microwaves carry signals between the ground and satellites in orbit. A dish on the ground transmits a microwave signal up to the satellite, which sends it back down to a receiver somewhere else on the Earth. Satellite television and satellite phone links work in this way.
A microwave oven cooks food using microwaves. The microwaves are absorbed by the food and the energy they transfer raises the temperature of the food.
Infrared – electrical heaters and cooking food

Electrical heaters such as radiant bar heaters, and cooking appliances such as grills, toasters and conventional ovens, emit infrared radiation. The infrared is absorbed by the surfaces it reaches – a person, a room, or the food – and transfers energy to them.

An infrared camera (a thermal imaging camera) detects the infrared radiation given out by objects and turns it into an image. Hotter and cooler parts of a scene show up differently, and no visible light is needed.
Fibre optic communications send information along very thin, very pure glass fibres as pulses of visible light. Telephone, television and broadband signals are carried this way.

An energy efficient lamp of the fluorescent type produces ultraviolet inside its tube. The ultraviolet is absorbed by a coating on the inside of the tube, and the coating gives out visible light, which is what lights the room.

Ultraviolet from the Sun, or from the lamps in a sunbed, is absorbed by the skin and makes it darken – a suntan. Ultraviolet is ionising, so this exposure also carries a risk of damage to skin cells and of skin cancer.

X-rays are used to form images of the inside of the body. They are transmitted through soft tissue but absorbed by denser material such as bone or metal, so a shadow image forms on the detector behind the patient. High-energy X-rays are also used in treatment, to destroy tumours.
Gamma rays – medical imaging and treatments

Gamma rays are used in medicine in two ways: a gamma-emitting tracer given to a patient can be detected from outside the body to show how an organ is working, and a beam of gamma rays can be directed at a tumour to destroy cancer cells.
Why radio waves suit television and radio

Radio waves have the longest wavelengths in the spectrum, so they spread around obstacles such as hills and buildings and reach receivers that are not in a direct line from the transmitter. They are not absorbed much as they travel, so a broadcast covers a large area, and they are not ionising, so broadcasting them over towns and cities is safe.

Microwaves pass through the Earth’s atmosphere, including the ionosphere, without being strongly absorbed or reflected, so a signal can travel up to a satellite and back down again. Longer-wavelength radio waves are reflected by the ionosphere and would not get through. Microwaves can also be sent as a narrow beam onto a dish, which keeps the signal strong.

The microwaves used in an oven are absorbed by water in the food, and the energy transferred raises the temperature of that water. Microwaves penetrate a few centimetres below the surface, so energy is transferred through a layer of the food rather than only to the outside, and conduction then spreads it to the rest.
Why infrared suits heaters and cooking food

Infrared is strongly absorbed by the surfaces of objects, including skin and food, and the energy transferred raises their temperature. Because it is a wave it travels directly from the heater or grill to whatever is in front of it, warming that object without having to warm the air on the way.

Every object emits infrared radiation, and a hotter object emits more of it, so a camera that detects infrared is detecting radiation the objects give out themselves. It therefore works in complete darkness, and differences in the infrared detected show up as differences in temperature.
Why visible light suits fibre optic communications

Visible light is hardly absorbed by very pure glass, so it travels a long way along a fibre without the signal fading. It is reflected from the walls of the fibre, so it stays inside and follows the fibre around bends instead of escaping. Its very short wavelength and high frequency allow a large amount of information to be carried.
Why ultraviolet suits energy efficient lamps

The ultraviolet made inside the lamp is absorbed by the coating on the tube, which gives out visible light. Almost all of the energy supplied is therefore transferred as light rather than being wasted heating a filament, which is what makes the lamp efficient. The coating and glass also stop the ultraviolet leaving the lamp.

Ultraviolet has a higher frequency and a shorter wavelength than visible light and is ionising, so when it is absorbed by the skin it can change the cells there, making them produce more dark pigment. Visible light and infrared from the Sun do not cause this change; infrared only warms the skin.

X-rays are transmitted through low-density soft tissue but absorbed by denser bone and by metal, so the pattern of radiation reaching the detector is a shadow of the structures inside the body. They travel in straight lines, so the shadow is sharp, and the image is obtained without any surgery.
Why gamma rays suit medical imaging and treatments

Gamma rays are very penetrating, so those emitted by a tracer inside a patient pass out through the body and can be detected outside it. They are also ionising and carry a great deal of energy, so a beam aimed at a tumour damages and kills the cancer cells there.

An optical component, usually of glass or plastic, that forms an image by refracting light. The light is refracted as it enters the lens and again as it leaves, and this change of direction is what brings the rays together or spreads them apart.

A lens that is thicker in the middle than at its edges. Parallel rays of light passing through a convex lens are brought to a focus at the principal focus, so a convex lens is also called a converging lens.

The point at which parallel rays of light are brought to a focus by a convex lens. For a concave lens, parallel rays are spread out so that they appear to come from the principal focus on the same side of the lens as the incoming light.

The distance from the lens to the principal focus. A more powerful lens, which bends light more strongly, has a shorter focal length. The focal length is a property of the lens itself and does not change when the object is moved.

The straight line drawn through the centre of the lens at right angles to it. Ray diagrams are set out along the principal axis, with the principal focus marked on it at the focal length from the lens on each side.
A lens that is thinner in the middle than at its edges. It spreads parallel rays of light apart, so it is also called a diverging lens, and the image it produces is always virtual.

A scale drawing that uses at least two rays from a point on the object to show where the image is formed, how big it is and which way up it is. Ray diagrams are used to show the formation of images by convex and concave lenses.

An image formed where rays of light actually meet after passing through the lens. Because the light really is there, a real image can be projected onto a screen. A real image formed by a convex lens is inverted.

An image formed where rays of light only appear to come from, once they are traced back behind the lens. No light actually meets there, so a virtual image cannot be projected onto a screen, although it can be seen by looking through the lens. A virtual image formed by a lens is upright.
Image produced by a convex lens

It can be either real or virtual. When the object is further from the lens than the principal focus, the refracted rays meet and a real, inverted image is formed. When the object is nearer to the lens than the principal focus, the rays leave still diverging and a virtual, upright, magnified image is formed on the same side as the object.
Image produced by a concave lens

It is always virtual. The refracted rays always leave the lens diverging, so they never meet; traced back, they appear to come from a point between the lens and the principal focus. The image is upright, smaller than the object and on the same side of the lens as the object.
Constructing a ray diagram for a convex lens

Draw the lens symbol on the principal axis and mark the principal focus at the focal length on each side. From the top of the object draw a ray parallel to the axis, refracted through the principal focus on the far side, and a ray straight through the centre of the lens, which is undeviated. Where these two rays cross is the top of a real image; if they do not cross, trace them back to find the virtual image.
Constructing a ray diagram for a concave lens

Draw the lens symbol on the principal axis and mark the principal focus on each side. From the top of the object draw a ray parallel to the axis, which is refracted so that it appears to come from the principal focus on the same side as the object, and a ray straight through the centre of the lens, which is undeviated. Trace the refracted rays back until they meet to locate the virtual image.

Both form images by refracting light, both are drawn on a principal axis with a principal focus at the focal length, and in both the ray through the centre of the lens goes straight on. They differ in what they do to parallel rays: the convex lens brings them to a focus, while the concave lens spreads them apart. Because of this the convex lens can produce a real or a virtual image, whereas the concave lens always produces a virtual one.

The magnification produced by a lens can be calculated using the equation: magnification = (image height)/(object height). This equation is supplied on the AQA Physics equation sheet, so the skill assessed is selecting it and applying it correctly rather than recalling it. A magnification greater than 1 means the image is larger than the object; a magnification less than 1 means it is smaller.

Magnification is a ratio — a height divided by a height — so the units cancel and the answer is a plain number with no unit after it. Writing '3 cm' or '3 mm' for a magnification is wrong; the answer is simply 3.
Measuring image height and object height

Image height and object height should both be measured in either mm or cm. What matters is that the same unit is used for both, because the ratio is only correct when the two heights are expressed in the same unit; if one is given in mm and the other in cm, convert one of them first.

In ray diagrams a convex lens is represented by a vertical straight line drawn across the principal axis with an arrowhead at each end, both pointing outwards, away from the axis. The outward arrowheads are a reminder that the lens is thicker in the middle.

A concave lens is represented by a vertical straight line drawn across the principal axis with an arrowhead at each end, both pointing inwards, towards the axis. The inward arrowheads are a reminder that the lens is thinner in the middle.

The band of electromagnetic waves that the human eye can detect, running from red at one end to violet at the other. It is a continuous spectrum: the colours run into one another rather than being separated by gaps.
Narrow band of wavelength and frequency

Each colour within the visible light spectrum has its own narrow band of wavelength and frequency. A colour such as red is therefore not one single wavelength but a small range of wavelengths, with a matching small range of frequencies.
Order of colours by wavelength and frequency

Across the visible spectrum, red light has the longest wavelength and the lowest frequency and violet light has the shortest wavelength and the highest frequency. Because all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed through a vacuum, a longer wavelength always corresponds to a lower frequency.
Reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction. Parallel rays arriving at a smooth surface, such as a mirror or still water, leave it still parallel, so a clear image can be seen.

Reflection from a rough surface causes scattering: this is called diffuse reflection. Parallel rays arriving at a rough surface, such as paper or matt paint, are reflected in many different directions, so no clear image is formed.
Law of reflection in diffuse reflection

Diffuse reflection does not break the law of reflection. At every point on a rough surface the angle of incidence still equals the angle of reflection; the surface is uneven, so the normals at neighbouring points face in different directions and the reflected rays are scattered.

A material that works by absorbing certain wavelengths (and colour) and transmitting other wavelengths (and colour). A red filter transmits red light and absorbs the other wavelengths; it does not create or add colour.
Light passing through a material and out the other side. Transmitted light is not changed into a different colour: its wavelength is the same on leaving the material as it was on entering.

Light energy being taken in by a material rather than being reflected or transmitted by it. Wavelengths that a filter or an opaque object absorbs do not reach the eye, so they make no contribution to the colour that is seen.

The colour of an opaque object is determined by which wavelengths of light are more strongly reflected. Wavelengths that are not reflected are absorbed, so a blue object reflects blue light strongly and absorbs the rest.

If all wavelengths are reflected equally the object appears white. A white object under white light therefore sends every wavelength back to the eye, which is why it takes on the colour of any coloured light shone on it.
If all wavelengths are absorbed the object appears black. Light does reach a black object; almost none of it is reflected back to the eye, so no colour is seen.

An object that transmits light without scattering it, so light passes through in a single direction and objects behind it can be seen clearly. Clear window glass and still, clean water are transparent.
An object that transmits light but scatters it as it passes through, so light gets through but objects behind it cannot be seen clearly. Frosted glass, tracing paper and thin fabric are translucent.
An object that transmits no light. Light falling on it is either reflected or absorbed, and it is the balance of those two that fixes the colour the object appears.

The idea that one object treats different wavelengths of light differently: it may reflect some strongly, absorb others and transmit others. The colour seen depends on which wavelengths actually reach the eye, so it depends on the object and on the light falling on it.
Viewing an object through a filter

What is seen depends on which wavelengths the object sends towards the filter and which of those the filter transmits. If the filter absorbs every wavelength the object reflects, no light reaches the eye and the object looks black.

Electromagnetic radiation emitted by every object because of its temperature. All bodies, no matter what temperature they are, both emit and absorb infrared radiation - a block of ice, a person and a hot oven are all emitting it at the same time as they absorb it from their surroundings.
Emission and absorption by all bodies

Emitting radiation means giving it out; absorbing radiation means taking it in. These happen together and continuously: an object does not have to be hot to emit, and it does not stop absorbing while it emits. What changes from object to object is the rate at which each happens.
Effect of temperature on the rate of emission
The hotter the body, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time. Two identical objects at different temperatures both emit, but the hotter one emits more radiation every second.

An object that absorbs all of the radiation incident on it. A black body does not reflect or transmit any radiation. It is an idealised object - a model - not simply an object whose surface happens to look black.

Radiation arriving at a surface can bounce off it (reflect), pass through it (transmit) or be taken in by it (absorb). A perfect black body does none of the first two, so all of the incident radiation is absorbed.
A good absorber is a good emitter

A surface that absorbs radiation well also emits it well. Since a perfect black body absorbs all of the radiation incident on it, it is the best possible absorber, and therefore a perfect black body would be the best possible emitter.

How much radiation a body emits - loosely, the energy radiated per second from each square metre of its surface. Intensity is one of the two things about an emission that depend on the temperature of the body.
