A body does not emit at one single wavelength. It emits over a range of wavelengths, with more intensity at some wavelengths than at others, and this spread is called the wavelength distribution. It is usually shown as a graph of intensity against wavelength.

The intensity and wavelength distribution of any emission depends on the temperature of the body. As a body gets hotter, the intensity increases at every wavelength and the peak of the distribution moves to shorter wavelengths - which is why a heated metal bar first feels warm, then glows dull red, then glows orange and finally white.

Any object in a room - a book, a wall, a person - is emitting radiation and absorbing radiation from everything around it at the same time. Explaining an everyday observation starts from that fact rather than from the idea that only hot objects radiate.

A body at constant temperature is absorbing radiation at the same rate as it is emitting radiation. Both processes are still happening; the two rates are simply equal, so the temperature does not change.

The temperature of a body increases when the body absorbs radiation faster than it emits radiation. If instead it emits faster than it absorbs, its temperature falls. It is the difference between the two rates that decides the direction of the change.

Some of the radiation arriving at the Earth is reflected straight back into space by clouds, by ice and snow and by other light surfaces. Radiation that is reflected is not absorbed, so it does not raise the temperature of the surface it bounced off.
Factors determining the temperature of the Earth

The temperature of the Earth depends on many factors including: the rates of absorption and emission of radiation, and reflection of radiation into space. The Earth's temperature settles where the total rate of absorption equals the total rate of emission back into space.

The same balance explains everyday cooling and warming. A hot drink emits faster than it absorbs, so it cools until the two rates match at room temperature; a car parked in sunshine absorbs faster than it emits, so it warms until the rising rate of emission catches up.

A typical diagram shows radiation from the hot Sun arriving mainly at short wavelengths; some is reflected back into space; the rest is absorbed by the surface and the atmosphere. The much cooler Earth then emits at longer infrared wavelengths, and gases in the atmosphere absorb some of this and re-emit it, part of it back towards the surface. Reading the arrows lets you compare the rates of absorption and emission.

permanent-and-induced-magnetism-magnetic.d: Permanent and induced magnetism, magnetic forces and fields
terms: A pole is a place on a magnet where the magnetic forces are strongest. A bar magnet has two: a north (seeking) pole and a south (seeking) pole, one at each end.
Like poles are two poles of the same kind (N and N, or S and S) and they repel each other. Unlike poles are one north and one south, and they attract each other.
A force that acts between two objects that are not touching. Attraction and repulsion between two magnetic poles are examples of non-contact force.
A magnet that produces its own magnetic field. It keeps that field whether or not any other magnet is nearby, and it has a fixed north pole and south pole.

A material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field. Induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction, and when the material is removed from the field it loses most or all of its magnetism quickly.
The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material.
A material on which a magnet exerts a force of attraction. The specification names iron, steel, cobalt and nickel.
The strength of the magnetic field depends on the distance from the magnet: it is strongest at the poles and gets weaker as the distance from the magnet increases.
The direction of the magnetic field at any point is the direction of the force that would act on another north pole placed at that point.

A line used to represent a magnetic field. Its direction is from the north (seeking) pole of a magnet to the south (seeking) pole of the magnet, and lines drawn closer together represent a stronger field.
An instrument containing a small bar magnet that is free to turn. The needle lines up with, and points in the direction of, the magnetic field it sits in.
The Earth has a magnetic field, and a compass needle placed away from other magnets points in the direction of the Earth's magnetic field.

A method of finding a field pattern: place a compass near the magnet, mark a dot at each end of the needle, move the compass so its tail sits on the previous head dot, repeat, then join the dots into a line and add an arrow.

A compass points the same way anywhere on the Earth's surface with no magnet nearby. The field must therefore be produced by the Earth itself, which is evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic.

Whenever a current flows in a conducting wire, a magnetic field is produced in the space around the wire. The field exists only while the current flows: switch the current off and the field disappears.
Field pattern around a straight wire

The field lines around a long straight current-carrying wire are concentric circles lying in a plane at right angles to the wire and centred on it. The circles are drawn close together near the wire and further apart further away, showing that the field is strongest close to the wire.
Factors affecting the field around a wire

The strength of the magnetic field around a wire depends on two things: the current through the wire, and the distance from the wire. A larger current gives a stronger field; moving further from the wire gives a weaker field.
Direction of the field around a wire

The direction of the circular field lines is shown by arrowheads and is given by the right-hand grip rule: point the right thumb along the conventional current and the curled fingers give the direction of the field lines. Reversing the current reverses every arrow.

A solenoid is a wire wound into a long coil of many turns. Shaping the wire this way increases the strength of the magnetic field produced by a given current, because the field of each turn adds to the field of its neighbours.

Inside a current-carrying solenoid the magnetic field is strong and uniform: the same strength and direction everywhere inside the coil. It is drawn as straight, evenly spaced, parallel lines running along the axis of the coil.

Outside the coil the field spreads out and has a similar shape to the field of a bar magnet, with one end of the solenoid behaving as a north pole and the other as a south pole. The lines outside run from the north end round to the south end, and every line is a closed loop that continues through the inside of the coil.

A core of iron placed inside a solenoid is magnetised by the field of the coil and greatly increases the strength of the magnetic field. Iron is used because it loses almost all of its magnetism as soon as the current is switched off.
An electromagnet is a solenoid with an iron core. Its magnetic field can be switched on and off with the current, and its strength can be changed by changing the current or the number of turns.

The magnetic effect of a current is demonstrated by placing plotting compasses, or scattering iron filings, near a wire and switching the current on: the compasses swing round to lie end to end along circles around the wire, and swing back to north when the current is switched off.

The magnetic effect of a current can be increased by increasing the current, by winding the wire into a solenoid with more turns so that the fields of the turns add together, and by adding an iron core.

In a relay a small current in a coil magnetises an iron core, which attracts a pivoted iron armature; the armature closes contacts in a second, separate circuit. A small current can therefore switch on a much larger one, and the two circuits stay electrically isolated from each other.

In an electric bell the current passes through an electromagnet that attracts an iron armature carrying a hammer; as the armature moves it breaks the circuit, the electromagnet switches off, a spring pulls the armature back and the circuit is remade, so the hammer strikes repeatedly.
When a conductor carrying a current is placed in a magnetic field, the magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on each other. This is called the motor effect.

Hold the thumb, first finger and second finger of the left hand at right angles to one another. The First finger points along the Field, the seCond finger along the Current, and the thuMb then gives the direction of the force, that is the Motion of the conductor.
Factors affecting the size of the force
The size of the force on a conductor in a magnetic field depends on the magnetic flux density of the field, the current through the conductor, and the length of conductor that is inside the field.
Magnetic flux density, symbol B, is the measure of the strength of a magnetic field used in this equation. It is measured in tesla, T, and a stronger magnet gives a larger flux density.
For a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field and carrying a current: force = magnetic flux density × current × length, written in symbols as F = B I l.
The tesla, T, is the unit of magnetic flux density. A flux density of 1 T gives a force of 1 N on each metre of a conductor carrying a current of 1 A at right angles to the field.
Symbols and units in F = B I l

Force, F, in newtons, N; magnetic flux density, B, in tesla, T; current, I, in amperes, A (amp is acceptable for ampere); length, l, in metres, m. Values must be substituted in these units, so a length given in centimetres has to be converted to metres first.

A coil of wire carrying a current in a magnetic field tends to rotate, because the forces on its two opposite sides act in opposite directions and so turn the coil about its axle. This is the basis of an electric motor.

The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn, just as the coil passes the vertical. The forces on the two sides therefore swap over at the right moment, and the coil keeps rotating in the same direction instead of stopping and rocking back.

A loudspeaker has a coil attached to a paper or plastic cone and sitting in the field of a permanent magnet. A varying current in the coil gives it a varying force by the motor effect, so the coil and the cone move in and out.

As the cone of a loudspeaker or headphone moves out and in it squashes and stretches the air next to it, producing the pressure variations that make up a sound wave. The frequency of the current sets the frequency of the sound and the size of the current sets the amplitude.

induced-potential-transformers-and-the-n.d: Induced potential, transformers and the National Grid (physics only) (HT only)
terms: If an electrical conductor moves relative to a magnetic field, or if there is a change in the magnetic field around a conductor, a potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor. If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, a current is induced in the conductor. This is called the generator effect.

The potential difference that appears across the ends of a conductor because of relative movement between the conductor and a magnetic field, or because of a change in the magnetic field around it. No cell is needed. A current is induced only if the conductor forms part of a complete circuit.

An induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change, either the movement of the conductor or the change in magnetic field. This is why a force must be applied, and work done, to keep a generator turning or to push a magnet into a coil.
Factors affecting the size of the induced potential difference

The size of the induced potential difference or induced current is increased by moving the conductor or magnet faster, by using a stronger magnetic field, and by using a coil with more turns. In short, the faster the magnetic field through the coil changes, the larger the induced potential difference.
Factors affecting the direction of the induced potential difference

The direction of the induced potential difference or induced current is reversed by reversing the direction of the movement, or by reversing the poles of the magnet, that is by reversing the direction of the magnetic field. Changing the speed or the number of turns alters only the size.

A generator that uses the generator effect to produce alternating current. A coil rotates in a magnetic field and is connected to the external circuit through slip rings, so each end of the coil stays joined to the same contact and the induced potential difference reverses every half turn.

A generator that uses the generator effect to produce direct current. A coil rotates in a magnetic field and is connected to the external circuit through a split-ring commutator, so the connections swap every half turn and the output potential difference never reverses.

The two continuous metal rings, one joined to each end of the rotating coil of an alternator, that keep each end of the coil connected to the same brush all the time. Because the connections never swap, the output alternates in direction as the coil turns.

The divided metal ring used in a dynamo. Every half turn each half of the ring meets the other brush, so the connections to the external circuit swap over at the moment the induced potential difference would otherwise reverse. The output therefore stays in one direction.
Potential difference against time graph for a generator

For an alternator the graph is a wave that rises and falls equally above and below the time axis, reversing every half turn. For a dynamo the graph is a series of humps all on the same side of the axis. Turning the coil faster makes the peaks both taller and closer together.

A device that uses the generator effect to convert the pressure variations in sound waves into variations in current in electrical circuits. The pressure variations make a diaphragm vibrate, the diaphragm moves a coil over a magnet, and the movement of the coil in the magnetic field induces a potential difference that varies in step with the sound wave.

A basic transformer consists of a primary coil and a secondary coil wound on an iron core. An alternating current in the primary coil produces a continually changing magnetic field in the core; that changing field passes through the secondary coil and induces an alternating potential difference across it. The two coils are not joined electrically.

The core on which the primary and secondary coils of a basic transformer are wound. Iron is used as it is easily magnetised, so it carries the changing magnetic field from the primary coil through to the secondary coil.

The ratio of the potential differences across the primary and secondary coils of a transformer Vp and Vs depends on the ratio of the number of turns on each coil, np and ns: Vp / Vs = np / ns, with potential difference, Vp and Vs in volts, V.

A transformer with more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil, so that in a step-up transformer Vs > Vp. Because the power output cannot exceed the power input, the secondary current is smaller than the primary current.

A transformer with fewer turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil, so that in a step-down transformer Vs < Vp. Because the power output cannot exceed the power input, the secondary current is larger than the primary current.

If transformers were 100% efficient, the electrical power output would equal the electrical power input: Vs × Is = Vp × Ip, where Vs × Is is the power output (secondary coil) and Vp × Ip is the power input (primary coil), with power input and output, in watts, W.

The unit of potential difference. In the transformer equation the potential difference, Vp and Vs, is in volts, V. A transformer changes the size of a potential difference; it does not change the unit it is measured in.
The unit of power. In the transformer power equation the power input and output, in watts, W, are each found by multiplying a potential difference in volts by a current in amperes.

Power is transmitted across the National Grid at a very high potential difference. For a given power transfer, Vp × Ip is fixed, so raising the potential difference lowers the current in the transmission cables. A smaller current wastes less energy heating the cables, which is the advantage of power transmission at high potential differences.

solar-system-stability-of-orbital-motion.d: Solar system; stability of orbital motions; satellites (physics only)
terms: One star, the Sun, together with the eight planets and the dwarf planets that orbit around the Sun, plus the natural satellites (moons) that orbit those planets.
A large body in orbit around the Sun. There are eight planets in our solar system.
A smaller body that orbits the Sun and is counted as part of the solar system but is not one of the eight planets.
A moon: a body that orbits a planet rather than orbiting the Sun directly. Natural satellites are part of the solar system.
A body, such as the Sun, in which fusion reactions release energy. Our solar system contains exactly one star.
The galaxy that contains our solar system. Our solar system is only a small part of it.
A cloud of dust and gas in space. The Sun was formed from a nebula pulled together by gravitational attraction.
The attractive force between masses. It is the force that pulls the dust and gas of a nebula together to begin a star.
The hot, dense body formed as gravity pulls a cloud of dust and gas together, before fusion reactions begin.
A reaction in which small nuclei join to form a larger nucleus, releasing energy. Fusion begins once gravity has made a protostar hot and dense enough.
The balance in a stable star between the gravitational collapse pulling it inwards and the expansion caused by the energy released by fusion.
The long, stable stage of a star's life during which the inward gravitational collapse and the outward expansion due to fusion energy are in equilibrium.
The sequence of stages a star passes through. Which sequence a star follows is determined by the size of the star.
The stage a star about the size of the Sun swells into when it leaves the main sequence.
The small, dense remnant left when a red giant of about the Sun's size collapses at the end of its life.
The cold, non-luminous remnant a white dwarf becomes once it has cooled down completely.
The stage a star much more massive than the Sun swells into when it leaves the main sequence.
The explosion of a massive star. It produces the elements heavier than iron and distributes all the elements throughout the universe.
The extremely dense remnant left at the centre after a supernova.
The remnant left after the supernova of the most massive stars, whose gravity is so strong that light cannot escape.
Fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements; elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova.
A man-made object placed in orbit around a planet, held in that orbit by gravity in the same way as a moon.
A path around a larger body in which the distance from that body stays the same, maintained by the force of gravity.
Speed is how fast something moves; velocity is speed in a stated direction. A change of direction alone changes the velocity.
An orbit that repeats indefinitely. For a stable orbit the radius must change if the orbital speed changes.

The observed increase in the wavelength of light from most distant galaxies. The same light, when produced on Earth, has a shorter wavelength, so features in the galaxy's spectrum are found nearer the red end. This effect is called red-shift.
The distance from one wave crest to the next. Visible light of longer wavelength lies towards the red end of the spectrum, so an increase in wavelength moves a spectral feature towards the red end.
Moving away from the observer. A galaxy that is receding shows an increase in the wavelength of its light, and the faster it recedes the bigger that increase is.

The way red-shift is observed. The pattern of lines produced by a known element on Earth is compared with the same pattern in the light from a galaxy; for a red-shifted galaxy the whole pattern sits at longer wavelengths.

The further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength. A bigger red-shift therefore means both a greater speed of recession and a greater distance.

The picture in which space itself grows, carrying the galaxies apart, rather than galaxies travelling out through a space that was already there. The change of each galaxy's speed with distance is evidence for it.
The theory that the universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense. The observed red-shift supports it, because an expanding universe must once have been very much smaller.

Scientists make observations, such as the red-shift of light from distant galaxies, and put forward a theory that explains them. The theory is then tested against further observations and may be developed or replaced.
Observations of supernovae made since 1998 onwards. They suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster, which changed what scientists say about how the universe is expanding.
Matter whose presence is inferred from its effects but which is not understood. The specification gives it as an example of how much about the universe is still not understood.
The name given to whatever is causing distant galaxies to recede ever faster. Like dark mass, it is given in the specification as an example of what is still not understood.

One of a small number of ideas used to describe the complex and diverse phenomena of the natural and man-made world. A key idea is a way of thinking that recurs across the whole subject rather than a detail belonging to one topic.

The property of the key ideas that they apply everywhere in the subject content rather than in one topic. Because they are embedded throughout the content, they underpin the assessment and are assessed across all papers.

A simplified representation of a system or process, used to describe, explain and predict behaviour. A model is judged by how well it explains and predicts, not by whether it contains every detail of the real thing.
A model in which matter is treated as a large number of small particles, with the arrangement and motion of those particles used to explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases.

A model in which a phenomenon is treated as a wave, so that quantities such as wavelength, frequency and amplitude can be used. Light is modelled as a transverse wave and sound as a longitudinal wave.
The idea that a change in one quantity produces a particular change in another: a resultant force causes acceleration, and a change inside an atomic nucleus causes a radioactive emission.
A phenomenon in which one object affects another without touching it, such as two magnets repelling, a charged rod attracting paper, or the Earth pulling on the Moon.

A region in which an object experiences a force because of a property it has, such as charge, magnetism or mass. The field concept is the key to analysing electrical, magnetic and gravitational effects.

A difference in a quantity between two places that causes something to change or to flow. A pressure difference drives gas flow, a temperature difference drives energy transfer by heating, and a potential difference drives charge flow.
A relationship in which one quantity changes by the same factor as another, so that the ratio of the two stays constant. Proportionality is an important aspect of many models in science.

The relationship shown by a graph that is a straight line through the origin. Weight is directly proportional to mass, and the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, up to the limit of proportionality.

The expression of a physical law or model as an equation relating quantities, for example weight = mass × gravitational field strength. The equation states the relationship itself, not merely a recipe for a calculation.

A system is an object or a group of objects. It is simply whatever you choose to treat as the thing being studied — a single stone, a stone and the Earth together, or a kettle together with the water inside it. Choosing the system first is what makes it possible to say clearly which stores are emptying and which are filling.

A way in which a system holds energy. Naming a store answers the question 'where is the energy now?' — for example the kinetic store, the gravitational potential store, the elastic potential store, the thermal store and the chemical store.
The store filled when an object moves. The faster the object moves and the greater its mass, the more energy is in its kinetic store.
The store filled when an object is raised. Its content depends on the mass of the object, its height, and the gravitational field strength.
The store filled when an object such as a spring, a rubber band or a crumpling car bumper is stretched, squashed or deformed.
The store filled when the temperature of a material rises. Almost every everyday change ends with energy in the thermal stores of the objects involved and of the surroundings.
The store held in fuels, foods and batteries, which empties when a chemical reaction such as burning or respiration takes place.
The moving of energy from one store to another. A transfer is not itself a store: the routes named in this section are heating, work done by forces and work done when a current flows.
A transfer of energy caused by a difference in temperature. Heating fills the thermal store of the cooler object and empties the store supplying the energy.
The transfer of energy that happens when a force moves an object through a distance along the line of the force. Work done is calculated using W = F s.
Work done when a current flows
The transfer of energy that happens when charge is pushed through a component by a power supply. The energy transferred in a time t is found from P = E / t.
The spreading out of energy into thermal stores of the surroundings, where it is no longer useful. The energy is still there; it is simply shared out too thinly to be used.
A diagram in which the energy in each store, before and after a change, is drawn as a bar using the same scale throughout, so that the redistribution of a fixed total can be seen at a glance.
The energy stored in an object because it is moving. It is calculated from kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x (speed)^2, that is E_k = 1/2 m v^2, and it is zero when the object is at rest.

In E_k = 1/2 m v^2 the speed alone is squared, not the mass and not the product of the two. Doubling the speed of an object multiplies its kinetic energy by four, while doubling its mass only doubles the kinetic energy.
Units in the kinetic energy equation
Kinetic energy Ek is in joules, J; mass m is in kilograms, kg; speed v is in metres per second, m/s. A mass in grams or a speed in km/h must be converted first, or the answer will not be in joules.

The unit of every energy store in this section: kinetic, elastic potential and gravitational potential energy are all measured in joules. The newton is a unit of force and the watt is a unit of power, so neither can be the unit of an energy calculation.

The energy stored in a spring, or other elastic object, because it has been stretched or compressed. For a spring it is calculated from elastic potential energy = 0.5 x spring constant x (extension)^2, that is E_e = 1/2 k e^2.
A measure of how stiff a spring is: the force needed for each metre of extension. It is measured in newtons per metre, N/m, so a spring of large k needs a large force to stretch it a given amount.

The increase in the length of the spring, measured in metres, m. It is the stretched length minus the original unstretched length, not the stretched length itself, and it must be converted from centimetres or millimetres before it is squared.

The point beyond which extension is no longer proportional to the force applied. The equation E_e = 1/2 k e^2 is used only while the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded; past that point it no longer gives the energy stored.

The energy stored in an object because of its position in a gravitational field. The amount gained when an object is raised is calculated from g.p.e. = mass x gravitational field strength x height, that is E_p = m g h.
The force acting on each kilogram of mass, measured in newtons per kilogram, N/kg. Its value is always supplied in the question in this specification, so it never has to be recalled.

The vertical distance the object is raised above ground level, measured in metres, m. When an object is moved along a slope or a ramp, it is the vertical rise that is used as h, not the longer distance travelled along the surface.
In E_p = m g h the gravitational potential energy Ep is in joules, J; mass m is in kilograms, kg; gravitational field strength g is in newtons per kilogram, N/kg; and height h is in metres, m.
Units in the elastic potential energy equation
In E_e = 1/2 k e^2 the elastic potential energy Ee is in joules, J; the spring constant k is in newtons per metre, N/m; and the extension e is in metres, m.
Mass is the quantity of matter in an object, measured in kilograms, kg, and it is m in all three equations. Weight is a force in newtons and is never substituted for the mass.

Use E_k = 1/2 m v^2 when an object is moving, E_e = 1/2 k e^2 when a spring has been stretched, and E_p = m g h when an object has been raised. Only the kinetic and elastic equations contain a factor of 0.5.
The object, or group of objects, whose energy is being considered. In this section the system is the material being heated or cooled — for example a metal block, or the water in a beaker.

The amount of energy stored in, or released from, a system as its temperature changes. Change in thermal energy, ∆E, is measured in joules, J. It is a change, not a total: it does not tell you how much energy the system stores altogether.

change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change. This is the equation used to calculate the amount of energy stored in or released from a system as its temperature changes.

∆E = m c ∆θ, where ∆E is the change in thermal energy in joules (J), m is the mass in kilograms (kg), c is the specific heat capacity in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius (J/kg °C) and ∆θ is the temperature change in degrees Celsius (°C). To find the specific heat capacity from measurements the equation is rearranged to c = ∆E ÷ (m ∆θ).

The mass of the material whose temperature changes, symbol m, measured in kilograms, kg. A mass measured in grams must be divided by 1000 before it is substituted into ∆E = m c ∆θ, because the unit of specific heat capacity is per kilogram.
Specific heat capacity (c) and its unit

Specific heat capacity, symbol c, is measured in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C. The unit is read directly from the definition: joules of energy, for each kilogram of substance, for each degree Celsius of temperature rise. It is a property of the substance, so its value does not depend on how much of the substance you have.

The specific heat capacity of a substance is the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius. The word 'specific' means 'per kilogram': the quantity is defined for a fixed one kilogram of the substance, not for the whole sample.

The difference between the final temperature and the starting temperature of the system, symbol ∆θ, measured in degrees Celsius, °C. It is a difference, so the value substituted into the equation is final temperature − starting temperature, never the final temperature on its own.

An investigation to determine the specific heat capacity of one or more materials. In a common version, the mass of a metal block is measured, an immersion heater and a thermometer are placed in the holes in the block, the block is lagged, the starting temperature is recorded, and the energy supplied by the heater and the temperature are recorded as the block warms. The specific heat capacity is then found from c = ∆E ÷ (m ∆θ). A version using a measured mass of water in an insulated container works in the same way.
Linking the energy stores in the practical

The investigation works by linking the decrease of one energy store (or the work done) to the increase in temperature, and so to the increase in the thermal energy stored by the material. With an electric immersion heater, the energy transferred from the supply is taken as the energy transferred to the material; the value of ∆E used in the calculation is that measured energy, read from a joulemeter or found from power × time.
Lagging and energy transferred to the surroundings

Insulating material (lagging) is wrapped round the block or container to reduce the energy transferred from it to the surroundings. Any energy that does escape was measured as supplied but did not raise the material's temperature, so the calculated specific heat capacity comes out higher than the accepted value. Lagging reduces this error; it never removes it completely.

Use of appropriate apparatus to make and record a range of measurements accurately, including mass, time and temperature. Here it means using a balance to measure the mass of the block or the water, and a thermometer or temperature sensor to record temperatures, with sensible precision and at recorded time intervals.

Safe use of appropriate apparatus to measure energy changes and transfers. Here it means setting up and using the immersion heater, the low voltage supply and the joulemeter (or ammeter, voltmeter and timer) safely — the heater must be in the block or water before it is switched on, and the hot block must not be handled — and using them to measure the energy transferred.

Opportunities include identifying the variables (energy supplied and temperature measured; mass and material controlled), evaluating the method by identifying energy transferred to the surroundings as a source of error, suggesting improvements such as better lagging or a smaller temperature range, and judging the result by comparing it with an accepted value for the material.

Opportunities include converting a mass in grams to kilograms, calculating ∆θ as a difference of two readings, rearranging ∆E = m c ∆θ to make c the subject, quoting the answer to a sensible number of significant figures with the unit J/kg °C, and plotting temperature against energy supplied and using the gradient of the straight line, which equals 1 ÷ (m c).

Power is the rate at which energy is transferred, or the rate at which work is done. It is not a quantity of energy: it says how many joules are transferred each second, so a power value always needs both an energy and a time.
The watt is the unit of power, symbol W. An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is equal to a power of 1 watt, so 1 W is 1 J/s.
The energy transferred, symbol E, is measured in joules, J. Divided by the time in seconds it gives the power: power = (energy transferred)/(time), [P = E/t].

Work done, symbol W, is measured in joules, J, because doing work is one way of transferring energy. Divided by the time it gives the power: power = (work done)/(time), [P = W/t]. The letter W is also the symbol for the watt; in P = W/t it stands for the work done.
The time, symbol t, is measured in seconds, s. A time given in minutes or hours must be converted to seconds before it is used in P = E/t or P = W/t.

Two machines that transfer the same energy, for example two electric motors lifting the same weight through the same height, differ in power only through the time taken. The one that finishes sooner has the greater power.

describing-motion-along-a-line.d: Forces and motion: Describing motion along a line
terms: Distance is how far an object moves along the path it actually travels. It does not involve direction, so it is a scalar quantity: a magnitude and a unit fully describe it, for example 450 m.

Displacement is the distance an object moves measured in a straight line from the start point to the finish point, together with the direction of that straight line. It is quoted as a magnitude and a direction, for example 450 m due east.
A scalar quantity has magnitude only. Distance and speed are scalars: stating the number and the unit says everything there is to say about them.
A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction. Displacement and velocity are vectors: two vectors of the same size pointing different ways are different quantities.
Speed is how fast an object is moving. It does not involve direction, so speed is a scalar quantity, measured in metres per second, m/s.
The specification gives typical values that may be taken as: walking about 1.5 m/s, running about 3 m/s and cycling about 6 m/s. These are estimates to be recalled and used, not exact figures.

Students should also be able to recall typical speeds for different types of transportation system, for example a car on a motorway at roughly 30 m/s, a train at roughly 50 m/s and an aeroplane at roughly 250 m/s.
The speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle depends on many factors including age, terrain, fitness and the distance travelled.

The speed of a moving object is rarely constant: when people walk, run or travel in a car their speed changes constantly. It is not only moving objects that have varying speed, because the speed of sound and the speed of the wind also vary.
A typical value for the speed of sound in air is 330 m/s. The actual value varies, for example with the temperature of the air.
Speed is found by measuring a distance, for example with a ruler, tape measure or trundle wheel, measuring the time taken with a stopwatch or light gates, and then dividing the distance by the time.
For an object moving at constant speed the distance travelled in a specific time can be calculated using distance travelled = speed × time, written in symbols as [s = v t].
Quantities and units in [s = v t]
In s = v t the distance s is in metres, m; the speed v is in metres per second, m/s; and the time t is in seconds, s.
For non-uniform motion the average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken, including any time spent stationary.
The velocity of an object is its speed in a given direction, so velocity is a vector quantity. Two objects with equal speeds have different velocities if they move in different directions.
Distance and speed are scalars; displacement and velocity are the matching vector quantities. Each pair has the same unit, and the vector member of the pair also carries a direction.

An object moving in a circle at a steady rate has constant speed but changing velocity, because its direction of motion changes continuously. Examples include a car on a roundabout and a satellite in a circular orbit.
If an object moves along a straight line, the distance travelled can be represented by a distance-time graph, with time on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis.

The speed of an object can be calculated from the gradient of its distance-time graph: gradient is the change in distance divided by the change in time. A horizontal line has zero gradient, so the object is stationary.
Tangent to a distance-time graph (HT only)
If an object is accelerating, its speed at any particular time can be determined by drawing a tangent to the curve at that time and measuring the gradient of that tangent.
Students should be able to draw distance-time graphs from measurements, and extract and interpret lines and slopes, translating information between graphical and numerical form.
The average acceleration of an object can be calculated using acceleration = (change in velocity)/(time taken), written in symbols as [a = (∆v)/(t)].
Acceleration, a, is in metres per second squared, m/s^2; change in velocity, ∆ v, is in metres per second, m/s; and time, t, is in seconds, s.
An object that slows down is decelerating. Its acceleration has the opposite sign to its velocity, so for an object moving forwards the acceleration is negative.
Students should be able to estimate the magnitude of everyday accelerations, for example a family car pulling away at roughly 2 m/s^2 and an object falling freely at about 9.8 m/s^2.

The acceleration of an object can be calculated from the gradient of a velocity-time graph. Students should be able to draw velocity-time graphs from measurements and interpret lines and slopes to determine acceleration.
Area under a velocity-time graph (HT only)

The distance travelled by an object, or the displacement of an object, can be calculated from the area under a velocity-time graph, and students should be able to interpret enclosed areas to determine it.
Where the area under a velocity-time graph is not a simple triangle or rectangle, it can be measured, when appropriate, by counting squares and multiplying by the quantity one square represents.
The following equation applies to uniform acceleration: (final velocity)^2 - (initial velocity)^2 = 2 × acceleration × distance, written in symbols as [v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s].
Quantities and units in [v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s]
Final velocity v and initial velocity u are in metres per second, m/s; acceleration a is in metres per second squared, m/s^2; and distance s is in metres, m.
Near the Earth's surface any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s^2, whatever its mass.

An object falling through a fluid initially accelerates due to the force of gravity. As it speeds up the drag force grows until eventually the resultant force is zero and the object moves at its terminal velocity. Physics only: students should be able to draw and interpret velocity-time graphs for objects that reach terminal velocity and interpret the changing motion in terms of the forces acting.

forces-accelerations-and-newton-s-laws-o.d: Forces and motion: Forces, accelerations and Newton's Laws of motion
terms: If the resultant force acting on an object is zero, the object's motion does not change: a stationary object remains stationary and a moving object continues to move at the same speed and in the same direction, so at the same velocity. The law is about the resultant of the forces being zero, not about there being no forces at all.

The single force that would have the same effect as all the forces acting on an object together. When the forces balance, that resultant is zero: a stationary object then remains stationary, even though individual forces such as weight and a surface's upward push are still acting on it.

Motion at the same speed in the same direction. If the resultant force on a moving object is zero, the object continues to move at the same speed and in the same direction, so it continues to move at the same velocity. No forward force is needed to maintain that motion.

When a vehicle travels at a steady speed the resistive forces balance the driving force. The driving force from the engine and the resistive forces of friction and air resistance are equal in size and opposite in direction, so the resultant force is zero and the velocity does not change.

The velocity (speed and/or direction) of an object will only change if a resultant force is acting on the object. A car rounding a bend at a constant speed has a changing direction, so its velocity is changing and a resultant force must be acting, even though the speedometer reading is fixed.

The tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion is called inertia. It is a tendency, not a force: passengers thrown forwards when a bus brakes are not pushed forwards, they simply keep moving at the velocity they already had while the bus slows beneath them.

The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force acting on the object, and inversely proportional to the mass of the object. Doubling the resultant force on a fixed mass doubles the acceleration; doubling the mass under a fixed resultant force halves the acceleration.

Newton's Second Law written as an equation: resultant force = mass x acceleration, F = m a. The F in the equation is the resultant of all the forces on the object, not any single force acting on it, and the equation can be rearranged to find the mass or the acceleration.

In the equation F = m a the force, F, is in newtons, N; the mass, m, is in kilograms, kg; and the acceleration, a, is in metres per second squared, m/s^2. A mass given in grams must be converted to kilograms before it is substituted into the equation.

Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object. A large inertial mass needs a large resultant force to produce a given change of velocity, which is why a loaded lorry is far harder to speed up or slow down than a bicycle.

Inertial mass is defined as the ratio of force over acceleration. Dividing the resultant force acting on an object by the acceleration that force produces gives the object's inertial mass in kilograms, which is the same rearrangement as m = F / a taken from F = m a.

Typical everyday values let speeds, accelerations and forces be estimated for road transport: a car reaching about 27 m/s in about 9 s accelerates at roughly 3 m/s^2, and with a mass of about 1000 kg that needs a resultant force of roughly 3000 N. Large accelerations demand correspondingly large forces.

The symbol ~ placed before a value indicates an approximate value or an approximate answer. Writing 'resultant force ~ 3000 N' says the figure is an estimate of the right order, obtained from rounded data, and not a precisely measured or exactly calculated result.
Required practical activity 7: force and acceleration

An investigation of the effect of varying the force on the acceleration of an object of constant mass. A trolley is pulled by hanging masses on a string over a pulley and the acceleration is found from light gate timings. The total mass being accelerated must be kept constant, so masses are moved from the trolley to the hanger to change the force.
Required practical activity 7: mass and acceleration

The second part of the same practical investigates the effect of varying the mass of an object on the acceleration produced by a constant force. With the pulling force fixed, extra masses are added to the trolley and the acceleration is measured each time; the acceleration falls as the mass rises, because acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.

Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite. If a swimmer pushes back on the water with 200 N, the water pushes the swimmer forwards with 200 N. The two forces are always the same size, whatever the sizes of the two objects.

In an equilibrium situation such as a book resting on a table, the third law pair is the book's downward push on the table and the table's upward push on the book. These act on different objects, so they never cancel; the book's weight and the table's upward push act on the same object and are balanced forces, not a third law pair.

forces-and-braking.d: Forces and motion: Forces and braking
terms: The total distance a vehicle travels from the moment the driver sees a hazard to the moment the vehicle comes to rest: stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.

The distance the vehicle travels during the driver's reaction time, before the brakes are applied. The vehicle is still moving at its full speed throughout, so thinking distance = speed x reaction time.
The distance the vehicle travels under the braking force, from the moment the brakes are applied to the moment the vehicle comes to rest.
Effect of speed on stopping distance

For a given braking force, the greater the speed of the vehicle the greater the stopping distance. Thinking distance grows in proportion to speed; braking distance grows faster still, because the same force must remove kinetic energy that depends on speed squared.

A rough stopping distance for a vehicle at a typical road speed, found by adding an estimated thinking distance (speed x about 0.7 s) to an estimated braking distance. For a car, about 23 m at 13 m/s (30 mph) and about 96 m at 31 m/s (70 mph).

A graph of stopping distance against speed for a vehicle. The thinking distance contribution is a straight line through the origin; the braking distance contribution curves upwards, so the total line gets steeper as speed increases. A heavier vehicle sits above a lighter one at every speed.
The time between a driver seeing a hazard and beginning to act on it. Reaction times vary from person to person, with typical values ranging from 0.2 s to 0.9 s.
Tiredness, drugs and alcohol lengthen a driver's reaction time. Distractions, such as using a phone or a loud conversation, may also affect the driver's ability to react.

A simple method of measuring human reaction time: one student releases a ruler between another's open finger and thumb without warning, and the distance the ruler falls before it is caught is converted into a time. A shorter drop means a shorter reaction time.

A method in which a computer displays a signal at a random moment and records how long the user takes to click. It gives a time directly in seconds and removes the human error involved in judging and converting a ruler drop.

Reaction time varies from trial to trial, so several trials are made and a mean is taken, with any anomalous result identified and excluded from the mean. This makes a comparison between two students, or before and after a change, more reliable.
Wet or icy road conditions reduce the grip between the tyres and the road, so the braking force that can be applied without skidding is smaller and the braking distance is longer.
For this specification, poor condition of the vehicle means worn or faulty brakes, or worn or badly inflated tyres. Either one increases the braking distance.

Because stopping distance grows sharply with speed, and grows further in poor conditions, safe driving means lowering speed and leaving a larger gap when the road is wet or icy, and keeping brakes and tyres in good order.
Work done by the braking friction force
When a force is applied to the brakes, work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle and the temperature of the brakes increases.
Braking force for a given distance
The greater the speed of a vehicle the greater the braking force needed to stop the vehicle in a certain distance, because more kinetic energy has to be removed over the same distance.
The rate at which a vehicle's velocity decreases. The greater the braking force the greater the deceleration of the vehicle.
Large decelerations require very large braking forces. These may lead to the brakes overheating and/or loss of control of the vehicle, for example if the wheels lock and the vehicle skids.

For a road vehicle the braking force can be estimated from the mass and the deceleration using F = m a, after finding the deceleration from the change in velocity and the time taken. Emergency braking of a family car gives decelerations of a few m/s2 up to about 10 m/s2 and forces of the order of 10 000 N.

transverse-and-longitudinal-waves.d: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Transverse and longitudinal waves
terms: A wave in which the oscillations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer. Ripples on a water surface are an example of a transverse wave.
A wave in which the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Longitudinal waves show areas of compression and rarefaction, and sound travelling through air is longitudinal.

The repeated back-and-forth or up-and-down movement of a particle of the medium about a fixed position as a wave passes. The direction of this oscillation compared with the direction the wave travels is what separates the two types of wave.
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles of the medium are pushed closer together than normal, so the medium there is at a higher pressure.

A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles of the medium are spread further apart than normal, so the medium there is at a lower pressure. The particles are still present; a rarefaction is not an empty space.
A wave on a water surface. Each part of the surface moves up and down while the ripple travels outwards, which is what makes it a transverse wave.
A longitudinal wave in which the air is repeatedly pushed together and pulled apart, producing compressions and rarefactions that travel away from the source.
A wave moves energy from place to place while the water or air it passes through only oscillates about a fixed position and is not carried along with the wave.

properties-of-waves.d: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Properties of waves
terms: Any wave, transverse or longitudinal, is described using four quantities: amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period. Amplitude describes the size of the oscillation; wavelength describes how long one complete wave is; frequency and period describe its timing and are two ways of stating the same information, since T = 1/f. Wave speed is a further quantity, but it is calculated from frequency and wavelength rather than being one of the four descriptive quantities.

The amplitude of a wave is the maximum displacement of a point on a wave away from its undisturbed position. It is measured from the undisturbed line up to a crest, or from the undisturbed line down to a trough — never from a trough all the way up to a crest, which is twice the amplitude. Amplitude is a distance and is read on the displacement axis of a wave diagram.

The undisturbed position is where a point in the medium would sit if no wave were passing — its rest position. On a wave diagram it is the centre line about which the wave oscillates, and it is the line from which amplitude is measured. Displacement is measured from this line, so a point at the undisturbed position has zero displacement even though the wave is still passing.

The wavelength of a wave is the distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave. Crest to the next crest, trough to the next trough, or any point to the matching point one wave later all give the same distance. Wavelength is given the symbol λ and measured in metres, m. A crest to the neighbouring trough is only half a wavelength.

The frequency of a wave is the number of waves passing a point each second. It is a counting rate — not a speed, and not a count of how many waves happen to be drawn on a diagram. Frequency is given the symbol f and measured in hertz, Hz, where 1 Hz means one complete wave passing each second.

The period of a wave is the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point, and it is the reciprocal of the frequency: period = (1)/(frequency). A high frequency therefore means a short period. A wave of frequency 8 Hz has a period of 1/8 = 0.125 s, because eight waves share each second.

The specification states the relationship as period = (1)/(frequency), in symbols [T = 1/f]. Because the two quantities are reciprocals, the relationship rearranges to f = 1/T, so either can be found from the other. A period of 0.004 s gives f = 1/0.004 = 250 Hz. Period and frequency are never equal in value unless both are 1.

The specification gives period, T, in seconds, s. Period is a time, so its unit is the second — the same unit as any other time interval. Periods of waves are often small fractions of a second, so answers such as 0.004 s are normal and should not be rounded to zero or converted into hertz.

The specification gives frequency, f, in hertz, Hz. One hertz is one complete wave passing a point each second. Larger frequencies are often quoted in kilohertz, kHz, or megahertz, MHz: 1 kHz = 1000 Hz and 1 MHz = 1 000 000 Hz, so a frequency in kHz is multiplied by 1000 to convert it into hertz before it is used in the wave equation.

The wave speed is the speed at which the energy is transferred (or the wave moves) through the medium. It is not the speed of the particles of the medium, which only oscillate about their undisturbed positions and are not carried along with the wave. Wave speed is given the symbol v and measured in metres per second, m/s.
All waves obey the wave equation

All waves obey the wave equation: it holds for transverse and longitudinal waves alike, and for waves in air, in fluids and in solids. Sound, ripples on water, waves on a string and electromagnetic waves are all covered by the same relationship, so a single equation links speed, frequency and wavelength for every wave met in this course.

The wave equation is wave speed = frequency × wavelength, in symbols [v = f λ]. It rearranges to f = v/λ and to λ = v/f. Because the speed is a product of the other two, a wave that keeps the same speed has a wavelength that falls as its frequency rises. Substituting f in Hz and λ in m always gives v in m/s.

The specification gives wave speed, v, in metres per second, m/s; frequency, f, in hertz, Hz; and wavelength, λ, in metres, m. The equation only produces a speed in m/s if the wavelength is entered in metres and the frequency in hertz, so a wavelength quoted in centimetres or millimetres must be converted first, and a frequency in kilohertz must be multiplied by 1000.
Reading amplitude and wavelength from a diagram

On a displacement–distance graph, amplitude is read vertically on the displacement axis, from the undisturbed centre line to a crest or trough, while wavelength is read horizontally on the distance axis, from one point to the equivalent point on the next wave. The two quantities are therefore measured on different axes, and confusing the axes is the commonest error when identifying them from a given diagram.
Measuring the speed of sound in air

A workable method is to stand a measured distance from a large reflecting wall, clap, and time the echo returning; the sound has travelled twice the distance to the wall, so wave speed = (2 × distance) ÷ time. Distances of many tens of metres, and timings taken over several claps, are used so that human reaction time is small compared with the time being measured. An alternative method uses two microphones a measured distance apart connected to an electronic timer.
Measuring the speed of ripples on a water surface

A ripple tank with a vibrating dipper produces ripples whose pattern is projected onto a screen below. The frequency is read from the signal generator driving the dipper, and the wavelength is measured with a ruler laid against the projected pattern, ideally across ten wavelengths which are then divided by ten. The wave speed is then found from v = f λ. A stroboscope or a video frame freezes the moving pattern so that it can be measured.
Sound passing from one medium to another

When a sound wave crosses from one medium into another, its frequency is fixed by the vibrating source and does not change. The wave speed does change, because it depends on the medium — sound travels faster in water, and faster still in solids, than in air. Since v = f λ and f is fixed, the wavelength must change in the same proportion as the speed: a faster medium gives a longer wavelength.

In this practical, observations are made to identify the suitability of apparatus for measuring the frequency, wavelength and speed of waves in a ripple tank and of waves in a solid, and appropriate measurements are taken. Typical judgements include using a ruler on the projected pattern rather than a stopwatch on a single ripple, reading the frequency from the signal generator, and measuring across ten wavelengths on a stretched string before dividing by ten.

reflection-of-waves-physics-only.d: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Reflection of waves (physics only)
terms: The surface where one material ends and a different material begins, for example air and glass or air and a brick wall. When a wave arrives at a boundary it can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted, and in most real cases all three happen at once in differing proportions.

The process in which a wave arriving at a boundary is sent back into the material it came from, rather than passing into the second material. Reflection happens at a boundary between any two different materials, not only at mirrors.
Reflection from a smooth surface, such as a plane mirror or still water. Parallel incident rays stay parallel after reflecting, so a clear image is formed.

Reflection from a rough surface, such as paper or a painted wall. The surface behaves as many tiny facets pointing in different directions, so parallel incident rays are scattered and no image is seen. The law of reflection still holds at every point.
The process in which the energy carried by a wave is transferred into the energy stores of the material at the boundary, usually the thermal energy store, so the wave itself does not continue.

The process in which a wave passes through the boundary and continues to travel inside the second material. A transmitted wave usually changes speed, and if it meets the boundary at an angle to the normal it also changes direction.

The change in direction of a transmitted wave at a boundary, caused by the change in the speed of the wave as it enters a different material. A wave travelling along the normal changes speed but does not change direction.

The construction line drawn at right angles to the surface at the point where the ray meets it, shown dashed in a ray diagram. Angles of incidence, reflection and refraction are all measured from the normal.
The angle between the incident ray and the normal at the point of incidence.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence. For any surface, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

A drawing showing the surface, the dashed normal at the point of incidence, the incident ray and the reflected ray, each drawn as a straight line with an arrow giving the direction of travel, with both angles marked from the normal.

What happens to a wave depends on the wave and on the two materials meeting at the interface. A matt black surface absorbs most visible light, a silvered surface reflects most of it, clear glass transmits most of it, and soft furnishings absorb much of the sound reaching them.

An investigation in two parts: shining a ray of light from a ray box at different types of surface and observing and measuring the reflected ray, then shining a ray into different transparent substances, such as a rectangular glass block or a perspex block, and tracing the refracted ray.

The technique of drawing round the block or surface, marking the incident and emerging rays with two pencil crosses set well apart, then removing the block and joining the crosses with a ruler so that the path inside the block can be drawn and the angles measured from the normal.

sound-waves-physics-only-ht-only.d: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Sound waves (physics only) (HT only)
terms: Sound wave travelling through a solid

A sound wave can travel through a solid, not only through air. As it passes, it causes vibrations in the solid itself: the particles of the solid are made to vibrate about their fixed positions and pass the disturbance on to their neighbours, so the wave is carried through the material.
A thin solid membrane inside the ear. A sound wave arriving at the ear drum makes it vibrate, so the ear drum is the point at which a sound wave in air is converted into vibrations of a solid.

Within the ear, sound waves cause the ear drum and other parts to vibrate, and it is this vibration that causes the sensation of sound. If the vibration is not produced, there is no sensation of sound.

The conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids works only over a limited frequency range: the solid parts involved can be made to vibrate by some frequencies but not by others. Outside that range the wave disturbance is not converted into vibration of the solid.

Because the ear drum and other parts of the ear only convert sound to vibration over a limited frequency range, human hearing has both an upper and a lower frequency limit. The range of normal human hearing is from 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), the number of waves passing a point each second. One kilohertz (1 kHz) is 1000 Hz, so the upper limit of normal human hearing, 20 kHz, is the same as 20 000 Hz.
Converting sound waves into vibrations of a solid

A process in which a sound wave in air arrives at a solid and makes that solid vibrate. Examples: sound waves striking the ear drum and making it vibrate; sound waves striking the diaphragm of a microphone and making it vibrate.
Converting vibrations of a solid into sound waves

The reverse process, in which a vibrating solid disturbs the air next to it and sends out a sound wave. Examples: the cone of a loudspeaker vibrating and producing sound waves in the air; a struck solid object vibrating and producing a sound.

waves-for-detection-and-exploration-phys.d: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Waves for detection and exploration (physics only) (HT only)
terms: Sound waves with a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans. Ultrasound is ordinary sound — a longitudinal wave that needs a medium — and differs from audible sound only in having a frequency too high for the human ear to detect.

The surface where one material meets a different material, for example soft tissue meeting bone, or one rock layer meeting another. Because the two materials carry the wave differently, a wave arriving at a boundary is changed there rather than passing through unaffected.

When a wave meets a boundary between two different media, part of the wave is reflected back and the rest carries on into the second medium. Ultrasound is partially reflected at every boundary it meets, which is why a single pulse can return several reflections from several depths.

The transfer of energy from a wave to the material it is passing through, so the wave becomes weaker as it travels. Different materials absorb a given wave by different amounts, and how strongly a signal has been weakened is itself information about what the wave has passed through.

The speed at which a wave travels is a property of the wave in a particular material, not of the wave alone. The same wave travels at different speeds in different materials, and it is this difference in velocity at a boundary that produces a reflection and reveals a hidden structure.

Using high frequency sound waves to detect objects in deep water and to measure water depth. A pulse is sent downwards, the time until its echo returns is measured, and the depth is found from that time — remembering that the pulse has travelled down and back.

A wave produced by an earthquake that travels through the Earth. Seismic waves are detected far from the earthquake, and which types arrive where is evidence about the material they have passed through.

A longitudinal seismic wave. P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids, so the times and directions in which they arrive carry information about the material deep inside the Earth.
A transverse seismic wave. S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, so a region of the Earth that receives no S-waves after an earthquake indicates liquid material somewhere on the path.

The central region of the Earth, which no one has ever seen or sampled. P-waves and S-waves provide the evidence for its structure and its size: S-waves failing to arrive shows liquid material, and the changing speed of P-waves shows where the core begins.

Evidence about something that cannot be observed directly, obtained by measuring what a wave does after passing near or through it. Ultrasound imaging, industrial testing and the study of the Earth's interior all rest on indirect evidence of this kind.

The use of ultrasound to build a picture of a structure hidden from view — an unborn baby or an organ in medicine, a crack or a flaw inside a metal casting in industry. Each reflection detected is turned into the distance to a boundary, and the set of distances becomes the image.
A transverse wave that transfers energy from the source of the wave to an absorber. Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum, so no substance is needed to carry them.
A wave in which the oscillations are at right angles to the direction in which the wave transfers energy. All electromagnetic waves are transverse.
A wave moves energy from one place to another without moving matter from one place to another. The particles or fields oscillate; they are not carried along.
The source is the object that emits the wave; the absorber is the object that takes in its energy. A lamp is a source of light; a black surface it shines on is an absorber.

The electromagnetic spectrum has no gaps: wavelength changes smoothly from very long to very short, and the seven named groups are labelled regions of one continuous range, not seven separate wave types.
The distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave. Radio waves have the longest wavelength in the spectrum and gamma rays the shortest.
The number of waves passing a point each second. Across the spectrum frequency rises as wavelength falls, so gamma rays have the highest frequency and radio waves the lowest.
The only group of electromagnetic waves the human eye can detect. Within it, red has the longest wavelength and violet the shortest, so the group runs red to violet.
A space containing no matter. All types of electromagnetic wave travel at the same velocity through a vacuum (space) or air, which is why sunlight reaches the Earth across empty space.

When a wave meets a substance and its energy is transferred into that substance rather than continuing through it. The wave does not emerge on the far side, and the internal energy of the substance rises.
When a wave passes through a substance and continues on the other side of it. A substance that transmits a wave allows it through with little of its energy being absorbed.
When a wave meets a boundary and is sent back into the substance it came from, instead of passing into the second substance.

The change in direction of a wave as it crosses the boundary between two different substances at an angle to the normal. A ray diagram shows it as the incident ray and the refracted ray making different angles with the normal.
Variation of these effects with wavelength

How a substance behaves towards electromagnetic waves is not a single fixed property of that substance. The same substance may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect waves of different wavelengths in different ways: glass transmits visible light but absorbs much of the ultraviolet reaching it, and brick transmits radio waves but not visible light.
Difference in velocity as the cause of refraction

Electromagnetic waves travel at different velocities in different substances. Some effects, refraction among them, are due to that difference in velocity: if the velocity of the wave is the same in both substances, no refraction occurs at the boundary between them.

A construction line drawn at right angles to the boundary at the point where the ray meets it, shown as a dashed line in a ray diagram. Every angle in a ray diagram is measured between a ray and the normal, never between a ray and the boundary.
Angle of incidence and angle of refraction
The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal. The angle of refraction is the angle between the refracted ray and the normal on the far side of the boundary.

A straight line with an arrow on it showing the direction in which the wave is travelling. A ray diagram of refraction shows the incident ray up to the boundary, the normal at that point, and the refracted ray continuing into the second medium.

Draw the boundary, then the normal as a dashed line where the incident ray meets it. A ray passing from air into glass or water bends towards the normal, so the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence. A ray passing from glass or water into air bends away from the normal. A ray that travels along the normal is not bent and carries straight on.

A line joining points on a wave that are all at the same point in their cycle, for example a line along a crest. Wave fronts are drawn at right angles to the direction in which the wave is travelling, and the distance between one wave front and the next is one wavelength.

When a wave front reaches the boundary at an angle, the end that crosses first changes speed first while the rest of the front is still travelling at the original speed. The front is therefore turned, and the direction of travel of the wave changes. In the medium in which the wave travels more slowly the wave fronts are drawn closer together, because the wave moves a shorter distance in each cycle; the frequency of the wave is unchanged.
Dependence of infrared absorption and emission on the surface

Every surface both absorbs and emits infrared radiation, but the amount depends on the nature of the surface. Matt, dark surfaces are the best absorbers and the best emitters of infrared radiation. Shiny, light-coloured surfaces are the poorest absorbers and the poorest emitters, and the best reflectors.

A sealed metal cube whose vertical faces carry different surfaces, typically matt black, matt white, shiny black and shiny silver. It is filled with hot water so that all four faces are at the same temperature, and an infrared detector held the same distance from each face in turn compares the radiation each surface emits.
Control variables in required practical activity 10

Only the nature of the surface may be changed. The distance between the surface and the detector or heater, the time for which readings are taken, the starting temperature, and the position and height of the detector must all be kept the same, or a difference in the readings cannot be attributed to the surface.

AT 1 covers the use of appropriate apparatus to make and record a range of measurements accurately. In this activity that means measuring distance with a ruler, time with a stopwatch, and temperature with a thermometer or infrared detector, and recording those readings to the resolution the instrument allows.

AT 4 covers making observations of the effects of the interaction of electromagnetic waves with matter. In this activity that means observing how infrared radiation interacts with surfaces of different nature — how much each surface absorbs when it faces a radiant heater, and how much each emits when it is hot.
WS and MS opportunities in this practical

The activity also gives opportunities to develop working scientifically skills, such as identifying control variables, judging the resolution and repeatability of measurements and evaluating the method, and mathematical skills, such as tabulating readings, calculating means and plotting temperature against time. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.

A repeated back-and-forth change of the current in a circuit, so that the charges move first one way and then the other, over and over. (HT only) Oscillations of this kind in an electrical circuit can produce radio waves.
(HT only) Radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits. The oscillating circuit is the source: the faster the oscillation, the higher the frequency of the radio wave produced.

(HT only) When radio waves are absorbed they may create an alternating current, so radio waves can themselves induce oscillations in an electrical circuit. Production and absorption are therefore two directions of the same link between radio waves and oscillating circuits.
Frequency of the induced alternating current

(HT only) The alternating current created when a radio wave is absorbed has the same frequency as the radio wave itself. A 200 kHz radio wave absorbed by a circuit induces an alternating current of 200 kHz.
Atoms and nuclei as sources of electromagnetic waves

Changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms can result in electromagnetic waves being generated or absorbed over a wide frequency range. The same atom can therefore be involved in emitting or absorbing radiation from very different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom. This origin, rather than any figure for frequency or wavelength, is what the specification uses to identify where gamma rays come from.

Radiation dose is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure of the body to radiation. It is not a count of the radiation itself: it combines how much radiation the body received with how damaging that type of radiation is.
The sievert is the unit in which radiation dose is measured. A dose quoted in sieverts tells you about the risk of harm from an exposure, so a larger number of sieverts means a greater risk of harm.

A smaller unit of radiation dose, used for the everyday doses people actually receive. 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), so to convert a dose in mSv to Sv you divide by 1000, and to convert Sv to mSv you multiply by 1000.
X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation. Being ionising is what makes them hazardous to human body tissue: they can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.
Ultraviolet waves can have hazardous effects on human body tissue: they can cause skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer.
A change to a gene caused by ionising radiation. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.

Using data you are given about radiation doses to compare exposures and comment on the risks and consequences. Doing this properly means converting all the doses to the same unit before comparing them, and stating conclusions as differences in risk rather than as certain outcomes.

uses-and-applications-of-electromagnetic.d: Uses and applications of electromagnetic waves
terms: Practical application of an electromagnetic wave

A use made of one group of the electromagnetic spectrum. The specification lists radio waves with television and radio; microwaves with satellite communications and cooking food; infrared with electrical heaters, cooking food and infrared cameras; visible light with fibre optic communications; ultraviolet with energy efficient lamps and sun tanning; and X-rays and gamma rays with medical imaging and treatments.

Radio waves are the longest-wavelength group of the spectrum and are used to broadcast television and radio programmes. A transmitter converts the signal into radio waves, and an aerial on a house or a receiver picks them up and converts them back.
Microwaves – satellite communications and cooking food

Microwaves have shorter wavelengths than radio waves. They are used to carry signals up to satellites and back down to earth, and in a microwave oven, where they are absorbed by the food and increase its energy store.

Infrared is emitted by all objects, and by more the hotter they are. It is used in electrical heaters and grills, where it is absorbed by the surface it falls on, and in infrared cameras, which form an image from the infrared an object emits.
Visible light is the narrow band of the spectrum the eye detects. In fibre optic communications, information is sent as very rapid pulses of light that travel along a thin glass fibre.
Ultraviolet – energy efficient lamps and sun tanning
