Ultraviolet has shorter wavelengths than visible light. It is produced inside an energy efficient (fluorescent) lamp and converted to visible light by the coating on the tube, and it is used in sunbeds and sunlight to tan skin, though it can damage skin cells.
X-rays and gamma rays – medical imaging and treatments

X-rays and gamma rays are the shortest-wavelength groups. They are used to make images of the inside of the body, because bone absorbs them far more than soft tissue does, and in treatment, where a beam is directed at a tumour to destroy its cells.
Absorption and transmission decide the use (HT)

Whether a wave is suitable for an application depends on what absorbs it and what lets it through. Microwaves suit satellite links because the atmosphere transmits them; infrared suits a grill because food absorbs it; X-rays suit imaging because bone absorbs them and flesh does not.

The layer on the inside of an energy efficient lamp that absorbs the ultraviolet produced in the tube and re-emits the energy as visible light, so the lamp lights the room without releasing ultraviolet into it.
A shaped piece of transparent material that forms an image by refracting light. The light changes direction as it enters the lens and again as it leaves, and that bending is what forms the image.
A lens that is thicker in the middle than at its edges. Rays of light arriving parallel to the principal axis are brought together to a focus at the principal focus.

A lens that is thinner in the middle than at its edges. Rays arriving parallel to the principal axis are spread apart, so that after the lens they appear to come from the principal focus on the same side as the object.
The straight line through the centre of the lens, at right angles to it, used as the reference line in every ray diagram.

The point on the principal axis at which rays of light that arrive parallel to that axis are brought to a focus by a convex lens. For a concave lens it is the point from which those rays appear to spread out.
The distance from the lens to the principal focus. It is a fixed property of a given lens: moving the object or the screen does not change it.
A drawing that uses straight lines with arrows to show the paths of selected rays of light, used to show how a lens forms an image and how large that image is.
An image formed where rays of light actually meet. Because the light really arrives there, a real image can be caught on a screen placed at that position.
An image formed where rays of light only appear to come from. The rays do not actually meet there, so no screen can catch it, but it can be seen by looking through the lens.
Image produced by a convex lens

It can be either real or virtual. With the object further from the lens than the principal focus the image is real and inverted; with the object nearer than the principal focus the image is virtual, upright and magnified.
Image produced by a concave lens
It is always virtual. Wherever the object is placed, the image is upright, smaller than the object and on the same side of the lens as the object.
Constructing a convex lens ray diagram

Two rays are enough. A ray from the top of the object parallel to the principal axis is refracted through the principal focus beyond the lens; a ray through the centre of the lens carries straight on. The top of the image is where they cross.
Constructing a concave lens ray diagram

A ray from the top of the object parallel to the principal axis is refracted so that it appears to come from the principal focus on the object side; a ray through the centre carries straight on. The image is found where the lines traced back cross.

How many times larger the image is than the object, calculated using magnification = (image height)/(object height). A value greater than 1 means the image is larger than the object; a value less than 1 means it is smaller.
Magnification is a ratio of two lengths, so the unit on the top cancels the unit on the bottom and the answer is a plain number with no unit attached.
Measuring image height and object height
Both heights should be measured in either mm or cm, and both must be in the same unit before they are divided, otherwise the ratio obtained is wrong.
In ray diagrams a convex lens is drawn as a vertical straight line with an arrowhead at each end pointing outwards, away from the principal axis.
In ray diagrams a concave lens is drawn as a vertical straight line with an arrowhead at each end pointing inwards, towards the principal axis.

The range of electromagnetic waves the human eye can detect, running from red at the long-wavelength end to violet at the short-wavelength end. The colours run continuously into one another rather than being separated by gaps.
Narrow band of wavelength and frequency

Each colour in the visible spectrum occupies a small range of wavelengths and a matching small range of frequencies, not a single value. Red occupies the longest-wavelength, lowest-frequency band; violet the shortest-wavelength, highest-frequency band.
Reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction. Parallel rays arriving at the surface stay parallel after reflection, so a clear image is formed, as in a plane mirror.

Reflection from a rough surface, which causes scattering. Each individual ray still obeys the law of reflection, but the surface normals point in many directions, so the reflected rays leave in many directions and no image is formed.
The spreading of reflected light into many directions, caused here by the unevenness of a rough surface. Scattering is why a sheet of paper looks equally bright from almost any viewing angle.

A material that absorbs certain wavelengths (and colours) of the light falling on it and transmits the other wavelengths (and colours). A filter removes light; it never adds light of a colour that was not already present.
The passing of light through a material, rather than the light being reflected from it or absorbed by it. Transmitted light emerges on the far side of the material.
The taking in of light energy by a material, so that the light does not leave the material as light. Wavelengths that are absorbed by an object are not available to be reflected or transmitted.
The fact that a single object treats different wavelengths differently, reflecting some strongly while absorbing others. This unequal treatment of the wavelengths is what gives an object its colour.
An object that transmits no light. Light falling on it is either reflected or absorbed, and its colour is set by the wavelengths it reflects most strongly.
A surface appears white when all wavelengths are reflected equally, and black when all wavelengths are absorbed. Black is therefore the absence of reflected light rather than a reflected colour.
Describes an object that transmits light without scattering it, so a clear image can be seen through it. Window glass and clear plastic are transparent.
Describes an object that transmits light but scatters it on the way through, so light gets through but no clear image can be seen. Frosted glass, tracing paper and thin fabric are translucent.
Colour of an object under coloured light
An object can only reflect wavelengths that are present in the light falling on it. If the illuminating light contains none of the wavelengths the object reflects, the object appears black.

A property of a moving object, defined by the specification as an equation: momentum is mass multiplied by velocity. Because velocity appears in the definition, an object has momentum only while it is moving, however large its mass is.
The word equation that defines momentum. It is one of the equations students must recall, so it has to be learned rather than looked up, and both quantities must be in SI units before it is used.
The symbol form of the definition: p stands for momentum, m for mass and v for velocity. Writing the symbols out before substituting keeps momentum separate from F = m × a, which shares the symbol m.
The unit of momentum. It is a compound unit built from the units of the two quantities being multiplied: kilograms for mass and metres per second for velocity, so kg × m/s = kg m/s.
In p = m v the mass, m, must be in kilograms. A mass quoted in grams or tonnes has to be converted first: divide grams by 1000, multiply tonnes by 1000.
In p = m v the velocity, v, must be in metres per second. A speed quoted in km/h is converted by dividing by 3.6. Velocity also has a direction, so momentum has a direction too.

A system in which no mass enters or leaves and no external resultant force acts. Conservation of momentum is stated by the specification for a closed system, and it is that condition which makes the total momentum before and after an event equal.

The name given to the statement that, in a closed system, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after the event. It applies to the total for the whole system, not to each object separately.

Anything that changes how the objects in a system are moving: a collision, objects sticking together, or an explosion pushing objects apart. Momentum is used as a model to describe and explain what happens in such an event.

An event in which objects initially at rest push each other apart. The total momentum before is zero, so the total momentum after must also be zero: the two objects move in opposite directions with momenta of equal size.
Newton's second law: the resultant force on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration. It is one of the two equations the specification combines to obtain the momentum form of the law.
The acceleration equation: acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken. Substituting it into F = m × a is what produces the momentum form of the second law.
The quantity m ∆ v, the mass multiplied by the change in velocity. Because momentum is m v, multiplying the same mass by the change in velocity gives the change in momentum, in kg m/s.
The equation formed by combining F = m × a with a = (v - u)/(t). The force equals the change in momentum divided by the time over which that change happens.

How quickly momentum changes, that is the change in momentum divided by the time taken. The specification states that force equals the rate of change of momentum, so the same change spread over a longer time means a smaller force.

When a force acts on an object that is moving, or able to move, the object's momentum changes. The force changes the velocity, and since momentum is mass × velocity with the mass fixed, the momentum must change with it.

Air bags, seat belts, gymnasium crash mats, cycle helmets and cushioned playground surfaces. Each one increases the time taken for the change in momentum to happen, which reduces the rate of change of momentum and so reduces the force.
Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths longer than visible light. Every object, at any temperature, emits and absorbs it.
The giving out of radiation by an object. All bodies emit radiation, and the hotter the body the more it emits in a given time.
The taking in of radiation incident on an object, so that energy carried by the radiation is transferred to the object.
An object that absorbs all of the radiation incident on it, reflecting none of it and transmitting none of it.
A surface that absorbs radiation well also emits it well, so a perfect black body would be the best possible emitter.
How much radiation a body emits per second. It increases as the temperature of the body increases.
How the emitted radiation is spread across a range of wavelengths. Its shape depends on the temperature of the body.
The wavelength at which a body emits most intensely. As a body gets hotter, the peak moves towards shorter wavelengths.
HT only. A body whose temperature is not changing is absorbing radiation at exactly the same rate as it is emitting radiation.
HT only. Absorbing radiation faster than it is emitted. The temperature of the body rises while this is happening.
HT only. Radiation turned back rather than absorbed. Radiation reflected into space never warms the Earth.
HT only. Set by many factors, including the rates at which radiation is absorbed and emitted and reflection of radiation into space.
